items.title: Chrysalis upgrades Starling valuation despite cut-price Boden sale
items.summary: Chrysalis Investments has lifted the value of its stake in Starling despite the recent cut-price share sale by the fintech’s founder Anne Boden. The British investment trust said on Monday its holding carried a price tag of around £403.9m, up by £47.9m following an external review. The trust holds around an 11 per cent stake [...]
items.body:
Chrysalis upgrades Starling valuation despite cut-price Boden sale
Chrysalis Investments has lifted the value of its stake in Starling despite the recent cut-price share sale by the fintech’s founder Anne Boden.
The British investment trust said on Monday its holding carried a price tag of around £403.9m, up by £47.9m following an external review. The trust holds around an 11 per cent stake in Starling, which would give the broader group a valuation of around £3.4bn when using Chrysalis’ benchmark.
It comes just weeks after news emerged that Boden, the group’s former chief executive, offloaded her remaining stake in Starling at a valuation of just £1.7bn marking a far cry from the £4bn the firm sought in a secondary share sale last year.
Chrysalis said it noted the speculation around Boden’s private sale but “considered its nature” and did “not believe that it impacts the company’s valuation”.
The London-listed tapped a strategy consultancy to conduct a new independent valuation review of Starling that split the business into two distinct parts: its digital bank and software-as-a-service platform Engine.
Analysts at Jefferies said the uprating was “at odds” with the valuation implied by Boden’s sale, but added they did not see the latter as “a meaningful valuation input given the small size of the transaction and as a sale of the last part of her stake.”
“Against this, the fact that the write-up was due to an independent valuation report is reassuring, although, in our view, the path to liquidity on the investment is still unclear,” they said.
Chrysalis brings in outsiders to value Starling
The report priced both parts of the business at five to six times their annual sales, based on what similar private tech firms are worth. This produced a higher valuation range, paving the way for the near £48m uplift in Chrysalis’ holding of Starling, which accounts for 65.6 per cent of its portfolio.
Chrysalis said it had adopted a valuation “at the midpoint of the report’s range”.
It follows the trust marking down its holding for two consecutive quarters this year, citing a decline in valuation multiples in its tracker set of high-growth fintechs and digital banks.
The group reduced the holding to £356m in the second quarter following successive five per cent and 14 per cent cuts.
Boden’s sale of her remaining Starling stake comes after she began recruiting software engineers for a project named ‘Moonshot’. She said she was seeking engineers who had a background in banking technology “who are excited about what the future could like”.
The founder’s cut-price deal is expected to add to investor concerns after Starling’s earnings slid over the last year. The firm posted a £217m pre-tax profit, down three per cent from the £223m secured in the prior year.

items.title: Retailers shift from smart trolleys to smart stores as Instacart shutters Caper Carts business
items.summary: In July, we reported that Morrisons had launched Instacart’s Caper Cart smart trolleys at a Preston supermarket, marking North American firm Instacart’s first retail partnership in the UK for its AI powered solution.Three months later, however, the retailer is pulling the trial as DoorDash gets set
items.body:
In July, we reported that Morrisons had launched Instacart’s Caper Cart smart trolleys at a Preston supermarket, marking North American firm Instacart’s first retail partnership in the UK for its AI powered solution.
Three months later, however, the retailer is pulling the trial as DoorDash gets set to acquire Instacart in a deal that values the grocery technology specialist at around $17 billion.
Separately, Instacart said in a regulatory filing last week that it would wind down its Caper Cart business by the end of the second quarter of 2027, expecting pre-tax charges of $55 million to $80 million related to the move.
Industry observers have been quick to write obituaries for the smart cart market over the past week. So are smart carts truly going away? The answer, according to Sandeep Unni, Retail Analyst at Gartner, lies in a detail that Instacart put out in its announcement: "While Caper is a great product, the business reality is that retailer adoption has not scaled quickly enough to justify our continued investment."
In a LinkedIn post, Unni said: "Translated, this points to a few structural challenges of an integrated hardware offering such as Caper. A Caper Cart can cost a grocer hundreds to thousands of dollars per cart plus maintenance, several orders of magnitude than a standard cart. Consequently, it proved that grocers are not keen to lock up capital into an expensive, proprietary hardware fleet."
He added: "A grocery store may have hundreds of shopping carts but only afford a few dozen Caper Carts, thereby limiting store level penetration. Grocers can solve the underlying checkout problem through alternative, less complex solutions without computer vision, sensor fusion and edge processing - retrofit smart cart handles, mobile scan and go apps, customer self-scanning solutions popular in Europe offer all offer much simpler, lighter tech alternatives and faster ROI."
Instacart's withdrawal is not a signal that smart carts have failed technically, Unni believes. Rather, it shows that the integrated smart cart model failed to become a sufficiently compelling enterprise scale investment in a segment with a razor thin margin profile.
"The market is shifting from "smart cart" to "smart store." Smart carts are simply one possible endpoint in a broader "store intelligence" strategy, not the strategy itself," he concluded.
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Smart carts will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
Check out our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
The awards, which celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world, have now closed for entries. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
The event will consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.

I'm sure my experience at Tesco, IGD and Advantage Group International will all serve me well. I've even managed to earn a few "cool points" from the kids for working for such a cool and popular brand. Wish me luck. As Domino's say, we got this."
Gaming
Domino’s is focusing on pizza lovers and gamers through a new collaboration with Minecraft Dungeons II.
Starting 26th October, customers who purchase a Domino, the brand’s new Detroit style pizza made for one, can get one of six collectible Minecraft Dungeons II themed pizza boxes, while Domino’s Rewards members who order online can unlock exclusive in-game items. Domino’s is also giving away 20,000 digital copies of Minecraft Dungeons II.
"We're always looking for new ways to bring customers closer to the brands and experiences they love,” says Kate Trumbull, Domino's Executive Vice President and Chief Marketing Officer.
“When we launched the Domino, we saw an opportunity to think beyond the pizza itself and create experiences that surprise and delight customers. Minecraft Dungeons II is all about teaming up with friends for epic adventures, and the Domino is built for those same moments. With its block shape and customisable toppings, it felt right at home in the game’s action packed universe, giving players an easy way to fuel up before jumping into battle.”
"With its block shape, playful spirit and perfect for gaming format, the Domino felt right at home in the Minecraft Dungeons II universe. Together, we're turning every purchase into an adventure, giving fans exclusive content, collectible items, and a chance to bring their love of pizza and gaming together. Whether you're teaming up with friends or braving the unknown, this partnership makes it even more rewarding to join the action.”
The Domino’s and Minecraft Dungeons II collaboration is part of a broader global roll-out covering: Australia, New Zealand, Belgium, Netherlands, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, Mexico, Portugal, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Spain, Taiwan, and Turkey.

items.title: Poundland founder Steve Smith blasts UK government and Gordon Brothers as retailer faces collapse
items.summary: Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, has taken to social media to hit out at the UK government and the retailer's current owner amid the discount chain filing notice to appoint administrators, bringing it one step closer to collapse.Earlier this year, Sky News reported that Gordon Brothers, Poundl
items.body:
Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, has taken to social media to hit out at the UK government and the retailer's current owner amid the discount chain filing notice to appoint administrators, bringing it one step closer to collapse.
Earlier this year, Sky News reported that Gordon Brothers, Poundland's owner for just 14 months at that time, had appointed Alvarez & Marsal to oversee an auction of the business. The US investment firm had paid a nominal sum of €1 for Poundland in June 2025, in a deal that promised up to £80 million in new funding but cut around 200 underperforming stores.
But last week Gordon Brothers filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the high court, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.
Only one bidder, Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family owned company, was interested in buying the entire chain and working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, the Chief Executive.
Gordon Brothers reportedly believes it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer, which was worth less than the £30 million in debt that Gordon Brothers took on when it bought the chain.
Poundland can be saved, Smith said in a LinkedIn post. He commented: "We started Poundland in 1990 and everyone said it will never work, here we are 36 years on. it wasn’t just me that created Poundland it was my staff, everyone contributed to making it what it is today."
"Everything the government has ever thrown at us, VAT increases, minimum wage increases and even business rate increases It has survived. 85% of the people in the UK have either been in or purchased something from a Poundland store. It has sold billions of pounds of products and created tens of thousands of jobs."
He added: "Over the last three months I got to know that Gordon Brothers were looking at selling the company. I tried several times to speak to them but they never returned my call. Because of this I was pleased that they must have had some good offers in that was acceptable to them. We now see that Gordon Brothers are looking at putting Poundland into administration."
"The big question is why? The business is performing well, almost 7% up on like for like sales. If Gordon Brothers are being greedy then it is going to cost thousands of jobs, in the newspapers it says 12,000 jobs are at risk. My estimate is more like 30,000 jobs. It is not just the people that work for Poundland it is also their suppliers, they have thousands of suppliers, some that just serve them, therefore these suppliers will suffer or be at risk of going into administration."
Poundland brings in millions of people every week into towns or shopping centres across the UK. Without this we will see lots of other retailers close down, Smith argues. "There is no high street revival without Poundland. If it goes into administration the suppliers will get next to nothing in the money they are owed and 12,000 people will lose their jobs, the only people that will make a lot of money out of this will be the liquidators."
"The government has been asked to get involved and the Prime Minister has already made contact. They need to take action not just say words. If Poundland closes down it will cost the tax payers billions of pounds, as up to 30,000 people will be looking for support as they will have no job."
Smith concluded: "A few years ago I tried to save Poundworld, it could have been saved but the owners found that they could make more money closing it down then saving jobs, what a disgrace. The government did nothing to help me save 7,000 jobs last time. Let’s see if the government does something this time."
"The Poundland management have put in a good offer for Poundland which will save the company. Let’s hope Gordon Brothers are not greedy and do the right thing by accepting their offer."

items.title: Five WordPress development companies for growing retail businesses
items.summary: For retail businesses, WordPress offers genuine flexibility when it comes to building and running websites, online shops, and wider digital experiences. It manages the early stages without much trouble. Growth changes the picture. Custom functionality, solid e-commerce connections, better performanc
items.body:
For retail businesses, WordPress offers genuine flexibility when it comes to building and running websites, online shops, and wider digital experiences.
It manages the early stages without much trouble. Growth changes the picture. Custom functionality, solid e-commerce connections, better performance, improved security, and consistent technical support move from nice-to-haves into necessities.
Pick the right WordPress development company and those gaps get filled while the site stays reliable and less of a pain to maintain. Get it wrong, and the problems just keep stacking up.
You’ll find specialist WordPress teams and full service digital agencies offering different strengths. Here are five that handle website development, customisation, integrations, and the steady improvements businesses need as they move forward.
How WordPress Development Supports Retail Growth
A retail website isn’t just a shop window with a buy button. It has to show the products properly, help people decide, talk to your stock system, and not fall apart on a phone.
A decent WordPress build can do the catalogues, the checkout, the payment links, and the CRM or email platform hook-ups. Make it fast and responsive so people don’t bounce. Keep it patched so it doesn’t get hacked.
What you actually need depends on what you’re trying to do and what you’ve already got. Find a developer who’ll cut the fluff and build the useful bits. Everything else is money down the drain.
Best WordPress Development Companies
The companies below provide different WordPress development capabilities. These range from custom website builds and complex integrations to ongoing maintenance and SEO support. Each one brings its own mix of services so businesses can select a partner that fits their technical requirements and growth plans.
The Site Slinger
The Site Slinger is a WordPress development company working with businesses, startups, SaaS teams, and agencies. The partner provides end-to-end WordPress development services, covering the full process from custom website builds and theme development to third-party integrations, ongoing maintenance, and technical support.
An exclusive WordPress focus gives clients access to a single senior team that stays with the site from start to finish. Building and launching the initial site, maintaining performance, and adapting it as requirements evolve all fall under the same group. Emphasis sits on clean code, dependable delivery, practical communication and maintainability over time.
Capabilities cover custom WordPress websites, turning AI generated designs into live production sites, custom themes, Figma-to-WordPress builds, connections to CRMs and other systems, and ongoing care. Every project remains with the same senior developers from the initial brief through launch and extended post-launch support.
WordPress Development Services
The Site Slinger covers a range of WordPress development needs, including:
- Custom WordPress Development: complete sites, custom functionality, WooCommerce, migrations, performance and security work
- AI Prototype to WordPress: Lovable, v0 and similar designs turned into production sites with a CMS you can actually use
- WordPress Theme Development: custom themes, reusable templates, Gutenberg blocks, editable components, structured content
- Figma to WordPress: approved designs built as responsive, CMS ready sites
- WordPress Integrations: CRMs, payments, marketing platforms, APIs, booking tools, other business systems
- WordPress Maintenance: updates, backups, security checks, monitoring, troubleshooting, improvements
Why Choose The Site Slinger?
If you’re after a proper long-term WordPress partner rather than separate teams for building and maintaining, Site Slinger is a solid shout. They only do WordPress, the same senior developers stay on your project, and they cover everything from the initial build through to post-launch support. It means the people who know the site keep looking after it as it expands and the requirements change.
GetDevDone
GetDevDone is a website development company helping agencies and brands build, improve, and scale websites, from web design to e-commerce and AI engineering in one team. It GetDevDone builds, customises, and maintains WordPress sites for businesses and agencies. Full process: custom builds, design conversion, theme and plugin work, migrations, integrations, ongoing support. Businesses agencies short on capacity get white label services, dedicated developers, and flexible engagement models.
The focus: stable builds, maintainable code, performance, security. Scoping, implementation, QA, testing, handoff. They'll also tackle site speed, search visibility, and content workflows, and cut unnecessary plugin dependencies.
WordPress Development Services
GetDevDone provides custom WordPress development services for projects of different sizes and technical requirements. Its main capabilities include:
- Custom WordPress Development: Sites, templates, and the specific functionality required
- Design to WordPress: Turning Figma and other design files into responsive websites
- Theme and Plugin Development: Custom themes, Gutenberg components, and tailored features
- Headless WordPress: Decoupled setups using React or Next.js
- Migration Services: Moving sites and content while protecting URLs and SEO
- Performance and Security: Speed work, access controls, and security patching
- Support and Maintenance: Updates, backups, bug fixes, monitoring, and continued improvements
Why Choose GetDevDone?
A solid option for businesses and agencies that need dependable WordPress development without growing the in-house team. White label services and flexible models slot developers into existing workflows. Maintainable code, performance, and security keep sites going long after launch.
WebDevStudios
WebDevStudios is an established WordPress development company founded in Pennsylvania by Brad Williams and Lisa Sabin-Wilson. Roots go back to the early days of WordPress, and they’ve built a strong reputation in the community. The founders are known for writing reference books on the platform. Clients include Microsoft, AT&T, the NBA, Campbell’s, and Discovery.
The company specialises in complex, custom coded WordPress solutions for enterprises, media and publishing businesses, technology companies, and large B2B brands. Expertise covers custom themes, complex WooCommerce projects, multisite networks, API integrations, data migrations, and performance optimisation. They also maintain tools in the WordPress ecosystem, including their AI powered WP Search plugin.
WordPress Development Services
End-to-end development from planning through maintenance. Capabilities:
- Custom WordPress Development: Tailored solutions for complex business needs
- WooCommerce Development: Custom e-commerce experiences and functionality
- Theme Development: Custom-coded WordPress themes
- Multisite Development: Building and managing multisite networks
- API Integrations: Connecting WordPress to external platforms and systems
- Data Migrations: Moving sites and data while handling the technical side
- Performance Optimisation: Improving speed and scalability
- Security and Maintenance: Ongoing support, security, and upkeep
Why Choose WebDevStudios?
A solid choice for enterprises and well-funded businesses with technically demanding WordPress projects. Experience, community reputation, and an engineering-focused approach make it worth considering for substantial customisation, complex integrations, or scalable architecture.
Simpalm
Simpalm’s a full service digital agency handling web and mobile solutions for enterprises, startups, and growing businesses. Over ten years at this. Specialises in WordPress development and custom software, building sites that scale properly, don’t annoy users, and actually perform.
They do more than WordPress. UI/UX design, mobile apps, custom web applications, digital transformation work. All aimed at digital experiences that keep customers engaged and help the business move forward. Clients include startups, nonprofits, healthcare and enterprise organisations.
WordPress Development Services
Simpalm pairs WordPress work with design and wider software skills. Main capabilities:
- Custom WordPress Development: Sites built to the actual business brief
- Responsive Web Design: Sites that work across screen sizes and devices
- WooCommerce Development: E-commerce functionality on WordPress
- UI/UX Design: Interfaces and user experiences that don’t frustrate people
- Mobile App Development: Apps built for business needs
- Custom Web Application Development: Web apps with the functionality required
- Website Maintenance and Support: Keeping sites running and updated
- Digital Strategy and Consultation: Straight advice on digital projects
Why Choose Simpalm?
Simpalm is worth considering for businesses that need WordPress development alongside design, mobile applications, or custom software services. Its broad service offering can be useful for organisations looking for a technology partner to support multiple parts of a digital project.
Visualwebz
Visualwebz is a Seattle-based web design and SEO agency that’s been specialising in WordPress development and search engine optimisation since 2008. They work with businesses after websites that mix responsive design with SEO done properly from the beginning.
They’ve worked with clients across healthcare, finance, education, sports and food. That includes responsive WordPress websites, ongoing site updates, and SEO strategies aimed at improving search visibility for the kind of industry-specific keywords that actually matter.
WordPress Development Services
Services include:
- WordPress Development: Building WordPress websites tailored to client requirements
- Responsive Web Design: Creating websites designed to work well across different devices and screen sizes
- SEO Friendly Website Development: Applying SEO considerations during development to support better search visibility
- Search Engine Optimisation: Developing strategies that attract relevant organic traffic and lift rankings for targeted keywords
- Website Updates: Maintaining and updating websites as client needs evolve
- Digital Marketing Support: Applying marketing expertise to help websites generate leads and improve conversions
Why Choose Visualwebz?
Visualwebz works well for businesses that want the WordPress development and the SEO coming from the same place. The combination of design, ongoing updates, and search optimisation suits outfits that need a solid working website plus proper support for organic visibility. One agency handling both sides of it.
Conclusion
Pick the right WordPress lot based on what you’re actually trying to achieve, what the tech needs to do, and where the business is headed. Some stick to proper WordPress builds and keep the site ticking over long-term. Others do white-label work, heavier engineering, full digital packages, or push the SEO side hard.
These five give you somewhere to start when you’re weighing up who can do what. Sit down with them first. Scope, timeline, budget, ongoing support - get it clear. Otherwise, you end up with something that works today and falls short the minute things change.

items.title: Best planogram software for grocery and convenience chains for 2026-2027
items.summary: Grocery and convenience chains plan shelves under tighter constraints than most retailers. A supermarket may carry 20,000+ SKUs across fresh, chilled, frozen, and ambient fixtures. A convenience store or fuel station shop squeezes a fast moving range into coolers, counters and a few short gondolas,
items.body:
Grocery and convenience chains plan shelves under tighter constraints than most retailers.
A supermarket may carry 20,000+ SKUs across fresh, chilled, frozen, and ambient fixtures. A convenience store or fuel station shop squeezes a fast moving range into coolers, counters and a few short gondolas, often with almost no backroom. When planograms for 50 or 500 such stores still live in Excel or Visio, every range change turns into weeks of manual redrawing, and nobody at head office knows what the shelves actually look like.
This guide compares seven planogram tools that grocery and convenience operators shortlist most often in 2026-2027. For each one, we cover what it does well, which store formats it fits, and what to check before you sign. The list starts with the platforms built for multi-store chains and moves toward tools focused on planogram design and category work.
What grocery and convenience chains need from planogram software
A drawing tool is not enough for a chain. These are the capabilities that separate a planogram system from a shelf-design app.
Store specific planograms from one master
No two stores have identical fixtures. The software should build a master planogram per category and adapt it automatically to each store's shelf lengths, cooler doors and local range, instead of a planner editing 60 files by hand.
Data driven facings
Facings should come from sales velocity, margin, days of supply and case pack, not from habit. For grocery this keeps fast movers like milk or bread from emptying by noon. For convenience it stops slow lines from blocking space in a 4-door cooler.
Fresh, chilled and specialist fixtures
Grocery planners need ambient shelving, chillers, freezers and hanging bars in the same library. Convenience and fuel retail adds coolers, counter units, tobacco gantries and promotional end caps.
Store execution and compliance
A planogram only works if it is on the shelf. Look for a mobile app that sends change tasks to store staff and checks shelf photos against the approved layout, ideally with image recognition.
Connection to inventory and replenishment
When shelf capacity and replenishment are planned in separate systems, stores get either overflow in the backroom or gaps on the shelf. Tools that share data with ordering, or plug into your ERP and PoS through APIs, avoid that conflict.
Fit for your chain size
Enterprise suites suit networks with large planning teams and long rollouts. Regional chains of 30 to 300 stores usually need something they can implement in months, not years.
Planogram software at a glance
The best planogram software for grocery and convenience chains
1. LEAFIO AI (Shelf Efficiency)
LEAFIO AI is a cloud platform for retail chains that combines planogram software for retail chains with inventory optimization and automated replenishment. Its planogram module, Shelf Efficiency, builds planograms from sales history, ABC classification and merchandising rules, then adapts them to each store's fixtures from one central library. Bulk updates let a category manager add or delist a product across the whole network in one step.
Execution is covered by a mobile app: store staff receive change tasks with visual instructions, photograph the shelf, and image recognition checks it against the approved layout. Because shelf capacity and replenishment run on the same data, facings and order quantities do not contradict each other.
For grocery and convenience, the published references are specific:
● Baltic Petroleum (86 fuel-station convenience stores, Lithuania) runs Shelf Efficiency together with inventory optimisation. In the first year the company reported +62% sales in planogrammed categories and a 50% cut in overstock across the network.
● Plum Market (US regional grocer) reported +11.4% sales and +12.3% profit over two years, and new-store preparation time fell from 14 to 4.5 days.
● Carrefour LabelVie (Morocco) is rolling out Shelf Efficiency across 180 stores in four formats, from convenience stores to hypermarkets.
These are vendor reported results. LEAFIO AI works with 250+ retailers in 45+ countries.
Best for: regional grocery and fuel-station chains of roughly 20 to 500 stores that want planograms, store execution and replenishment in one system.
Watch out for: pricing is quoted per project, so budget comparisons need a demo and a proposal.
2. RELEX Solutions
RELEX is a unified retail planning platform where planograms, floor plans, assortment, forecasting and replenishment share one data model. It is a common choice for large convenience networks: Kwik Trip selected RELEX in 2022 for automated planograms and floor planning across 850 stores, and Casey's adopted its space planning and supply chain platform for more than 2,400 stores in 2023.
The strength is integration. Space decisions feed directly into ordering, fresh and promotion planning, and store teams get planograms on mobile.
Best for: large grocers and c-store chains running a broader supply chain transformation.
Watch out for: scope and implementation effort are significant, which can be more than a regional chain needs if the goal is mainly better planograms.
3. Blue Yonder Space Planning
Blue Yonder builds assortment driven, store specific planograms and floor plans and connects them to its category management and retail planning suite. Recent additions include an AI assistant that edits planograms through plain-language requests, and a mobile app that guides in-store setup and checks compliance from shelf photos. Its customer list includes grocers such as Tesco and Morrisons and the convenience chain RaceTrac.
Best for: enterprise grocers with large category teams and complex fixture rules.
Watch out for: enterprise licensing and a longer learning curve. Smaller chains may pay for capabilities they will not use.
4. NIQ Spaceman
Spaceman is one of the longest established planogram tools and is widely used by category managers and CPG suppliers, especially those already working with NIQ market data. In October 2026 NIQ added conversational AI for building planograms, automated store-specific planograms (which NIQ says are up to 50 times faster to create) and AI compliance measurement, with NIQ-hosted cloud access.
Best for: analyst led category teams and suppliers preparing shelf recommendations for retailers.
Watch out for: confirm which of the new automation features are included in your package and how store execution is handled.
5. DotActiv
DotActiv combines planogram design, assortment analysis and store clustering, backed by a long category management consulting background. It publishes its license pricing, from a free edition up to an Enterprise AI tier, so it is easy to evaluate before talking to sales. It also offers outsourced category planning for teams without in-house planners.
Best for: mid-size grocers and suppliers that want structured category management at a predictable cost.
Watch out for: the core application is desktop-based, and link to replenishment depends on your other systems.
6. Quant
Quant generates store-specific planograms automatically from templates and keeps floor plans (macro space) and shelf planograms (micro space) in one application. It supports shelving, gondolas, freezers, hanging systems and pallets. Planograms are published to stores through Quant Web, where staff can add photos of the finished shelf. The Retail Planning plan includes unlimited users.
Best for: chains with many store layouts that want floor and shelf planning together.
Watch out for: check how deep the integration with your ordering process goes if shelf capacity should drive replenishment.
7. PlanoHero
PlanoHero is a web-based planogram and floorplan tool aimed at small and mid-size chains. It includes a mobile app for store teams and a built-in AI assistant for shelf placement suggestions. Pricing starts at $199 per month on the Lite plan, with enterprise pricing on request and a free trial.
Best for: smaller grocery and convenience chains that want to move off spreadsheets quickly.
Watch out for: fewer enterprise references and lighter analytics than the larger platforms.
Best planogram software by retail format
Best for supermarket and grocery chains
For regional supermarket chains of 30 to 300 stores, LEAFIO AI and RELEX are the strongest options when planograms must match fresh and ambient replenishment.
LEAFIO AI is faster to implement for mid-size chains; RELEX fits better when space planning is part of a wider supply chain project. National grocers with large category teams should add Blue Yonder to the shortlist.
Best for convenience stores and fuel station retail
Convenience formats need compact, store specific layouts and strong store execution, because stores have little staff time for resets. LEAFIO AI has documented fuel station deployments in the Baltics, including Baltic Petroleum, where planograms and automated ordering run on the same platform. RELEX is proven at very large US networks such as Kwik Trip and Casey's. Smaller c-store chains starting from spreadsheets can look at PlanoHero.
Best for chains with many store formats
If one chain runs hypermarkets, supermarkets and convenience stores, template-based automation matters most. Quantkeeps floor plans and shelves in one tool, and LEAFIO AI generates format specific planograms from one library, as in the Carrefour LabelVie roll-out across four formats.
Best for category teams and suppliers
NIQ Spaceman and DotActiv suit analyst led category work, supplier presentations and teams that rely on syndicated market data.
How to choose planogram software for your chain
- Define the main problem. Slow planogram production, poor store compliance and shelf gaps caused by ordering need different strengths. Write down which one costs you most.
- Shortlist three vendors that fit your size. A 40-store chain and a 2,000-store network should not run the same selection.
- Run the same test with each vendor. Give them one real category, such as dairy or soft drinks, with your product data and fixture sizes. Ask them to build a master planogram, adapt it to three store formats, push a range change to all stores and show the compliance check.
- Pilot in 5 to 10 stores. Measure planner hours per planogram, time to roll out a change, compliance rate and out-of-stocks against comparable control stores.
- Check the integration last, but check it properly. Confirm how sales, stock and item data flow in from your PoS and ERP, and whether planogram capacity reaches your ordering process.
FAQs
What is the best planogram software for a convenience store chain?
For regional convenience and fuel station chains, LEAFIO AI is a strong fit because it links planograms with automated store ordering and has fuel-station references such as Baltic Petroleum. For networks of 800+ stores running a wider supply chain project, RELEX is the common choice. Small chains moving off spreadsheets can start with PlanoHero.
What is the best planogram software for supermarkets?
Mid-size supermarket chains usually compare LEAFIO AI and RELEX, both of which connect shelf space with replenishment. Large national grocers often add Blue Yonder. Quant suits chains with many different store layouts.
How much does planogram software cost?
It ranges widely. DotActiv publishes per-license pricing that starts with a free edition, and PlanoHero starts at $199 per month. LEAFIO AI, RELEX, Blue Yonder and NIQ quote per project, based on the number of stores, categories and modules.
Can planogram software check store compliance?
Yes. Most chain level tools now include a mobile app where staff photograph the finished shelf. LEAFIO AI, Blue Yonder and NIQ Spaceman use AI image recognition to compare the photo with the approved planogram and flag wrong products, facings or gaps.
How long does implementation take?
For a regional chain, a pilot on a few categories and stores typically takes weeks to a few months, followed by a phased roll-out. Enterprise suites that also cover supply chain planning take longer. Ask each vendor for a timeline based on a chain of your size.

items.title: Just one country remains in Tesco’s decades-long global retreat
items.summary: Tesco’s sale of its Czech and Slovak businesses is the latest step in its long retreat from a once-sprawling global presence. Felix Armstrong traces this journey Tesco’s hold on the British grocery market is unmatched. Holding a towering 27.8 per cent market share across more than 3,600 shops, the supermarket chain is a fixture on [...]
items.body:
Just one country remains in Tesco’s decades-long global retreat
Tesco’s sale of its Czech and Slovak businesses is the latest step in its long retreat from a once-sprawling global presence. Felix Armstrong traces this journey
Tesco’s hold on the British grocery market is unmatched. Holding a towering 27.8 per cent market share across more than 3,600 shops, the supermarket chain is a fixture on high streets and retail parks across the UK.
But the UK was once just a small part of the grocer’s global geographic footprint, spanning Arizona to Malaysia.
The firm’s ambitions for expansion across the world had once been sky-high. In 2007, then-chief executive Sir Terry Leahy said there was nowhere the grocer wouldn’t go. “We are on the threshold of becoming one of the few successful international retailers. There’s plenty to do,” he had said.
Under the stewardship of Ken Murphy, however, Tesco performed a handbrake turn. The group has gradually retreated from more than a dozen international markets, as its boss focuses his efforts on pushing down prices and improving quality at home.
The far-flung countries from which Tesco has packed up its belongings in recent years include Poland, Thailand, China, Turkey, Pakistan, the US, Hong Kong and South Korea.
And following the FTSE 100 group’s £1.5bn sale of its businesses in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, just one trace remains of Tesco’s globetrotting escapade: Hungary.
Murphy told shareholders on Friday that it had been “a privilege to serve customers” in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, adding that he was “proud” of what Tesco had achieved in the two markets.
But he said the sale of these two businesses will allow the grocery chain to double down on its “core UK and Irish businesses and [support] our continued investment in our food-first retail ecosystem and the capabilities that will drive future growth, while enabling a further return of capital to shareholders”.
Tesco first acquired its store estate in these two countries as a by-product of its exit from Taiwan, when it swapped its footprint in the East Asian state with French retailer Carrefour’s shops in the Czech Republic and Slovakia.
Last year, Tesco’s operations in these two countries accounted for £2.9bn in revenue, across their combined 363 locations.
Orbán to blame?
The grocer had been expecting to offload its Hungarian arm as part of a wholesale exit from central Europe, but it said on Friday that it is continuing to “review all options for the future of [its] business in Hungary”.
It is unclear whether Tesco offered its Hungarian operations to Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch supermarket which picked up the rest of its European arm, or whether the grocer has opted to retain its last outpost on the continent.
Charles Allen, an analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said he thinks Tesco “would like” to sell its business in Hungary but is being blocked from doing so by the heavy tax burden which faces retailers in this market.
Hungarian Prime Minister Victor Orbán has led a campaign against foreign-owned food sellers in recent years. In 2022, his government slapped a 4.5 per cent tax on revenues generated by these firms, along with a requirement to lower the prices of a number of staple foods.
In March last year, Orban capped grocery markups on 30 basic food items – including eggs, milk and meat – at 10 per cent above wholesale costs in a bid to clamp down on rampant inflation.
Supermarket chains including Austrian-owned Spar have hit out at the Hungarian government for its “devastating” tax hikes, appealing to the European Union to intervene.
The 4.5 per cent tax has “pushed many chains into loss,” Allen said. He suggested that Tesco has adopted a ‘wait-and-see’ approach in the hopes that measures to soften these pressures could make the Hungarian market “more investor friendly.”
Tesco told shareholders on Friday that its businesses in the Czech Republic and Slovakia account for the “majority” of the £119m underlying profit generated by its central European arm, suggesting that its stores in Hungary are feeling the pinch.
Selling off its Hungarian outpost would leave Tesco with only Ireland as its sole territory outside the UK, where it controls roughly a quarter of the market. But given Murphy’s Cork roots, that arm of the business is going nowhere fast.

items.title: Who will be the AI winners this holiday season?: last week's most read retail technology articles
items.summary: Check out our most clicked retail technology articles from last week, including Morrisons, Instacart, DoorDash, Gap Inc., lululemon, Shopify, Just Eat, Revolut, Strawberry, TFG London, and the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.Morrisons bins Instacart AI powered Caper Carts trial amid DoorDash acquisition
items.body:
Check out our most clicked retail technology articles from last week, including Morrisons, Instacart, DoorDash, Gap Inc., lululemon, Shopify, Just Eat, Revolut, Strawberry, TFG London, and the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
Morrisons bins Instacart AI powered Caper Carts trial amid DoorDash acquisition talks
In July, we reported that Morrisons had launched Instacart’s Caper Cart smart trolleys at a Preston supermarket, marking North American firm Instacart’s first retail partnership in the UK for its AI powered solution.
Three months later, however, the retailer is pulling the trial as DoorDash gets set to acquire Instacart in a deal that values the grocery technology specialist at around $17 billion. Separately, Instacart said in a regulatory filing on Monday that it would wind down its Caper Cart business by the end of the second quarter of 2027, expecting pre-tax charges of $55 million to $80 million related to the move.
The plan is to reinvest any savings into strategic growth initiatives, which includes other in-store solutions like smart price tags and computer vision technology to help grocers track in-store inventory.
Responding to the news, retail analyst Steve Dresser said on LinkedIn: "Not one to mock innovation, it's vital. But this was always overplayed and seemed to be a chance for people to get their name in lights, rather than a meaningful trial to scale."
lululemon taps Shop Pay from Shopify across retailer's US and Canadian e-commerce sites
lululemon has announced the addition of Shopify's Shop Pay solution to its Canada and US e-commerce sites.
"We strive to meet our guests where they are, with an online experience that is thoughtful, secure, and easy to use,” says Nick Engel, SVP Global Digital Experience, lululemon.
“Shop Pay has earned its place in how people shop online, creating the kind of checkout where hundreds of small details come together into something that just works. Bringing it to lululemon.com in the US and Canada gives our guests a familiar, trusted way to complete a purchase, and takes one more step out of the path to getting what they came for.”
Customers can access one-tap checkout, saved payment and shipping details, and order tracking in the Shop app.
"lululemon sets the bar for brand experience, and checkout is one of the most important moments in the online purchase process,” says Lauren Nemeth, VP Global Enterprise, Shopify. "Shop Pay is already trusted by hundreds of millions of shoppers - now lululemon can offer it on top of their existing infrastructure.”
John Lewis, Asda, Morrisons, H&M, Dunelm, and Waitrose among 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards finalists
We're hugely pleased to present the finalists and shortlists for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards, sponsored by 3D Cloud, Business France, and Retail Technology Show 2027. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! Our winners will be announced this week at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Fashion retailer Gap Inc. starts scaling Bridgette, an AI tool for seasonal hiring, across stores and DCs
Gap Inc. has started to scale Bridgette, an AI enabled virtual career guide for seasonal hiring, across its stores and distribution centres.
Bridgette answers candidate questions at any hour, coordinates interviews and sends reminders. In a pilot, nearly 45,000 candidates engaged with it, and it has scheduled more than 7,000 interviews for store leaders.
In a LinkedIn post, Sven Gerjets, EVP and CTO at Gap Inc., said: "It works every day of the week, which is a better schedule than mine. What I care about most is what it does not do. Managers still run the interviews and make the hiring decisions. That is the point."
He added: "Our approach to AI is human centred and digitally enabled. For every step in a process, we ask what should be automated, what should be AI assisted, and what should stay with a person. Then we redesign the work around the outcome instead of speeding up the old process."
"Hiring is a good example, because the repetitive coordination was crowding out the conversations that build great teams. I keep coming back to a simple test. Does the technology give people their time back for the human work that matters most?"
McKinsey research shows retailers are losing the start of the shopping journey to AI tools
29% of AI shoppers say AI chat or search tools had the biggest influence on their most recent purchase - three times the share citing traditional search engines (9%), and more than retailers’ platforms and AI assistants combined (21%), according to new McKinsey & Company research drawing on a survey of approximately 21,000 consumers in 11 markets.
The shift is moving beyond discovery to influence and transactions. In the US, the share of AI users completing a purchase through AI has surged 70% since December 2025, from 10% to 17%.
Kelsey Robinson, Senior Partner, McKinsey & Company, says: "Consumers are showing unmet appetite and preference for AI shopping. Nearly a third of AI shoppers said AI chat or search tools were the biggest influence on their recent purchase. The winners this holiday season will be those that have stood up an agentic capability and are treating this as an always-on experimentation muscle."
Revolut Pay one-click account-to-account payments go live on Just Eat app and online
Just Eat has announced a partnership with Revolut, meaning that the on demand delivery big hitter's customers can now select Revolut Pay for a one-click checkout experience within its app and online in the UK and Ireland.
To mark the launch, users can earn a 5x RevPoints boost on every Just Eat purchase between 28th October and 27th December. Following the promotional window, customers will retain a 2x points boost on every purchase, alongside the ability to instantly redeem RevPoints for cash discounts at the Just Eat app and web checkout.
Selecting this option means that customers will no longer need to manually input card details and can authorise restaurant and grocery orders using biometric authentication (Face ID or fingerprint recognition) through their Revolut account.
Michiel Verberg, Head of Global Strategic Partnerships at Just Eat, says: "We're always looking for ways to make ordering from Just Eat faster and more rewarding. Revolut Pay removes a step from checkout, and the RevPoints boost gives customers something back on every order. This is the start of two of Europe's leading technology companies building a better user experience together, which is good news for consumers."
Swedish startup Strawberry launches AI agent platform and preps Series A funding round
Strawberry, a startup with $6 million in funding from EQT and General Catalyst, has launched 1.0 of its AI agent platform built for non-technical teams, such as sales, recruiting, customer support and marketing.
It is free to try and lets users and teams create their own virtual colleagues, called AI companions. According to Strawberry, unlike chatbots such as Claude and ChatGPT, which take a prompt and complete a task, companions work like real colleagues, alongside people and not instead of them. It operates as a browser, where a team's context, workflows and logins already live. A companion remembers how your team works and gets better the more you work together, because it is connected to all of that context.
"The technology is already here: agents can now work for weeks in a row. Yet, we see so many companies struggle with adoption. We built a product so delightful that teams adopt it naturally, with companions you bring into your team like colleagues," says Charles Maddock, CEO and Co-founder at Strawberry.
"Today the person who is great with Claude keeps all of it on their own laptop. In Strawberry you train a companion once, and everyone on the team gets it, with everything it has learned. The browser is fast becoming the front line for AI, and the Strawberry team is at the centre of that shift," says Yuri Sagalov, Partner, General Catalyst.
The Stockholm, Sweden-based company plans to follow this launch with a Series A funding round.
Phase Eight owner TFG London contacts customers as personal data is accessed following cyber attack
The owner of Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight has contacted its customers following a cyber security incident earlier this month and urged them to be alert to unexpected emails, calls or text messages.
TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - identified an incident on Sunday, 11th October affecting some IT systems and specifically impacting the Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles fashion brands.
In an email sent to customers, dated 28th October, TFG London CEO Justin Hampshire said: "On identifying a cybersecurity incident affecting some of our IT systems, we acted immediately to secure our systems, brought in independent cybersecurity experts, and notified the relevant government authorities."
He added: "Unfortunately, our investigation has shown that some personal data has been accessed, and we wanted to contact you about this as soon as we could. We are contacting all of our customers as a precaution. This does not mean that your information was affected, and our investigation into exactly which information has been accessed is continuing."
The information affected could include contact and delivery details, order information, and in some cases limited payment information, such as the last four digits of a payment card. It doesn't include useable payment card details.

items.title: Retailers say Budget will make it harder to hire young people
items.summary: Writing in the Daily Mail, BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson said higher costs and the rising tax burden make it harder to hire, with 'serious consequences' for young people.
items.body:
Retailers say Budget will make it harder to hire young people
The Budget has made it harder for businesses to take on more staff with young people set to bear the brunt, according to High Street bosses.
In a stinging rebuke to Andy Burnham and John Healey, the British Retail Consortium (BRC) said that instead of offering businesses ‘breathing space’, the Chancellor heaped more difficult costs onto employers.
Writing in the Daily Mail, BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson said higher costs and the rising tax burden make it harder to hire, with ‘serious consequences’ for young people.
She said that Healey had ‘made it more expensive to employ people, operate stores and invest, risking higher prices for households.’
And this comes as retailers stand ready to help with a worrying crisis of young people out of employment, offering them a ‘vital first step’ into the working world.
But Labour ‘risks finding itself hamstrung by its own Budget’ as the Government's own policies make it ‘harder to provide’ opportunities to young workers.
Retailers have warned that the rising cost of doing business will have ‘serious consequences’ for young people.
‘But as employment costs rise, those opportunities become harder to provide,’ she said.
The BRC, whose members include Marks & Spencer, Tesco and B&Q owner Kingfisher, has said that the ‘smoke and mirrors’ Budget has added another £250million to retailers’ business rates bills next April.
This is despite the Chancellor hailing a move to take 70,000 additional small businesses out of paying rates altogether and to freeze rate increases for other retailers in real terms.
Although the BRC had asked for no increase whatsoever, bills will go up by 3.5 per cent, in line with inflation.
Higher rates come hand-in-hand with a £2billion hike in employment costs after a 3.9 per cent increase to wages.
‘Retailers want to pay their colleagues well, but there is a limit to what they can absorb without sacrificing jobs and investment,’ Dickinson said.
Firms ‘desperately needed breathing space from this Budget’ after being hit with mounting costs over the past two years, including £6.5billion in additional employment costs relating to previous Budgets, she said.
Workers’ rights reforms will also ‘add to these pressures’, Dickinson said, pointing to
warnings from The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) that proposals could ‘weigh further on the labour market’.
Extra costs are also coming down the line because of the impact of the war in Iran and extreme weather conditions on supply chains.
British retailers’ electricity bills are set to rise by £440million this year, with more than half the cost made up just from levies and taxes.
Dickinson added that the Government’s ‘policies must match its promises’ and called for a reduction in the costs of hiring young people and an overhaul of business rates.
Retailers have called for the threshold to start paying employer National Insurance contributions to be raised. This would make more young people’s jobs exempt from the payments.
Before the Budget, M&S boss Stuart Machin said the threshold being cut 'hit shops hard, because so many of our jobs are entry-level and part-time, often just a shift or two a week'.
Chancellor Healey failed to deliver breathing room for Britain’s high streets
By Helen Dickinson, Chief Executive of the BRC
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has urged the Government to do more to help the High Street.
Britain’s high streets desperately needed breathing space from this Budget. Instead, Chancellor Healey has handed them another bill.
One in seven shops stands empty, more than 120,000 retail jobs have disappeared in two years, and retailers face £41billion in business taxes this year alone. Instead, the Chancellor has made it more expensive to employ people, operate stores and invest, risking higher prices for households.
Take business rates. The Chancellor announced that rates for retail, hospitality and leisure would be frozen in real terms. But dig into the detail and this supposed freeze actually means a 3.5 per cent increase, adding another £250million to retailers’ bills next April.
Removing 70,000 small high street businesses from paying business rates altogether is welcome. But hundreds of thousands of medium and larger retail outlets, responsible for most retail jobs and business rates contributions, will see their bills rise again. Retail accounts for just 5 per cent of the economy but pays more than 20 per cent of business rates.
Employment costs are rising too. Retailers have absorbed £6.5billion in additional employment costs over the past two years, and this Budget adds another £2billion. Retailers want to pay their colleagues well, but there is a limit to what they can absorb without sacrificing jobs and investment.
Some of Labour’s upcoming employment reforms will add to these pressures, with the OBR warning that the Employment Rights Act reforms could “weigh further on the labour market”, with increased uncertainty, reduced flexibility, and higher costs potentially outweighing productivity gains.
That has serious consequences for young people. Almost one million are not in education, employment or training, and retail has long provided a vital first step into work, offering the experience and skills needed to build a career. But as employment costs rise, those opportunities become harder to provide.
With Alan Milburn’s review of youth unemployment due to report soon, Labour risks finding itself hamstrung by its own Budget. Ministers may identify ways to get more young people ready for work, but their own policies risk leaving businesses less able to provide those opportunities.
Retailers are determined to tackle this challenge. Through Opening Shift, more than 40 leading retailers have pledged over 11,000 work experience placements, part of the industry’s wider ambition to create 100,000 jobs for young people not in education, employment or training by the end of this Parliament.
Yet while retailers are taking action, the Chancellor has missed an opportunity to back them.
Raising the threshold at which employers start paying National Insurance contributions, particularly for younger workers, would have helped businesses create more entry-level jobs. Instead, further action could be delayed until the 2027 Budget. Young people cannot afford another year of inaction.
Nor are employment costs the only challenge. Retail electricity bills are expected to rise by £440million this year despite almost no change in usage, with more than half the cost made of levies and taxes. Yet the industry remains excluded from Government schemes aimed at high-energy-use businesses.
Each decision adds to the cost of running a retail business. Together, they leave less money to open stores, invest in communities and create jobs. And with billions in additional costs, more of these pressures risk feeding through into shop prices, making the fight against inflation even harder.
Chancellor Healey has got himself into a pickle: promising to revive Britain’s high streets while piling more costs onto the businesses that keep them alive.
Retailers share the Government’s ambitions for thriving high streets, more jobs and growth in every postcode. They are already doing their bit, investing in communities and creating opportunities for young people.
Now the Government must do its bit. That means reducing the cost and risks of hiring young people, reforming business rates and restoring confidence to invest. If Labour is serious about giving breathing room to Britain’s high streets, its policies must match its promises.

items.title: M&S adds punch to its Christmas campaign with Amandaland star weeks after celebrity-studded fashion show
items.summary: The FTSE 100 store has recruited Lucy Punch, star of the sitcom Amandaland, as the face of its Christmas advertising campaign.
items.body:
M&S adds punch to its Christmas campaign with Amandaland star weeks after celebrity-studded fashion show
Party frocks and seasonal treats such as Snow Much Fun pudding will take centre stage when Marks & Spencer unveils plans this week to add sparkle to its Christmas.
The FTSE 100 store has recruited Lucy Punch, star of the sitcom Amandaland, as the face of its Christmas advertising campaign.
There may also be an appearance by fellow actress Gillian Anderson, who fronted Marks & Spencer’s successful ‘Love That’ fashion campaign.
The update will come as M&S delivers its half-year results on Wednesday with 54 days to go until Christmas.
Trading in the six months to September, when temperatures soared, drove demand for skimpier outfits and salads.
Thanks to lighter dishes and a growing number of customers doing their full weekly shop at its stores, M&S was named Britain’s fastest-growing grocer.
Kate Calvert, head of retail and consumer research at Investec bank, forecast pre-tax profits of £397million, more than double the previous year’s £184million, although last year M&S was reeling from a serious cyber-attack that forced the suspension of its online and click-and-collect orders.
In charge: Stuart Machin, chief executive of M&S, has ambitious plans for the business
Calvert expects a 12.5 per cent increase in food sales to £252million and a 20 per cent jump in food, home and beauty sales to £197 million.
M&S chief executive Stuart Machin has emphasised the focus on food, home and beauty, saying ‘the hard yards start here’.
In September, M&S launched its first catwalk show at London Fashion Week, with half the collection from the fashion show costs under £50.
Models at the fashion show included Lara Stone, Jodie Kidd and Erin O'Connor, while guests such as Dame Joan Collins, Jessie Ware, David Gandy, Katherine Jenkins, Jamie Redknapp and Kelly Hoppen watched on from the front row.
M&S began selling ready-made petticoats, pullovers and underwear in 1926, and paved the way to make everyday fashion affordable to the British public on the High Street.
Christmas cheer: M&S has recruited Lucy Punch, star of the sitcom Amandaland, as the face of its Christmas advertising campaign
Fashion show: Kemi Badenoch and Dame Joan Collins at the M&S fashion show in September
Machin said: 'We started selling fashion 100 years ago with our first products being everyday essentials – from poplin jumpers and pleated dresses to socks and sleepwear.
'We added more categories and more fashion and M&S became known for bringing style to the High Street – always with brilliant quality and value.
'Our transformation is building the business we want to be tomorrow, but it starts with our heritage. "Protect the magic, modernise the rest" means protecting what has made M&S special for 100 years and putting fantastic products at the heart of everything we do.
'Our first London Fashion Week collection is designed around that DNA; fashion that is stylish but wearable, made with outstanding quality and always value for money.'
John Lyttle, managing director of fashion, home and beauty at M&S, said in September: 'The show reflects the progress we have made, but it is not an end point.
'There is much more to do as we continue to invest in our stores, modernise our supply chain and strengthen our data and digital capability.'

items.body:
Tesco’s 2026 Christmas advert ‘The Wrong Address’ launches today, with a story about rekindled friendships, relatable mistakes, and some extra little helps from Tesco. The three-minute long film stars award-winning comedian and actor Roisin Conaty as Polly, a Tesco delivery driver who after many years unexpectedly crosses paths again with old school friend Lizzie, played by highly acclaimed actor Anna Maxwell Martin.
Receiving your big Tesco delivery at Christmas is an essential part of millions of Christmases in homes up and down the UK. When Lizzie accidentally orders hers to her old address, it creates the perfect level of jeopardy to kick off this year’s Tesco Christmas ad.
Given her new address is hundreds of miles from the one her delivery has arrived at, Lizzie is in despair. At the other end of the country, Tesco delivery driver Polly doesn’t want to let Lizzie’s family go without their Christmas treats, so she offers to help get Lizzie’s groceries closer to home. What should be a simple handover halfway turns into an unexpected reunion road trip as the protagonists reminisce and reconnect whilst making the epic road trip to deliver Christmas.
Earlier this year, Tesco launched its ‘Need Anything from Tesco?’ campaign platform which has helped tell the stories of how Tesco has shown up for customers throughout 2026- from quality food, great value on the essentials every week, and its community programme Free Fruit and Veg for Kids. This Christmas story is a continuation of Tesco’s commitment to supporting every customer, across every moment of the year.
Roisin Conaty said: “I love that this story centres on female friendship. It starts in a way many people can relate to, all stress and mayhem, but shows how one small act of kindness can bring people back together after years apart. It’s lovely to show Polly and Lizzie reuniting and celebrating kindness and grace. Also, the silliness we can only feel with old friends alongside the magic of Christmas.”
Anna Maxwell Martin said: “We’ve all been there. In the stress to get everything perfect at Christmas, suddenly you realise you’ve somehow only ordered one singular sprout, totally forgotten wrapping paper, or sent a delivery to the wrong address. I’m really pleased to be part of a production that acknowledges that whilst we can all strive for our ‘perfect’ Christmas, it is in fact human connection that truly helps to make Christmas magic.”
Suzanne Quinn, UK customer director at Tesco said: “This Christmas, Tesco is showing up with plenty of extra little helps to deliver customers their very best Christmas. Whether that’s cracking deals on the products they love, delicious, exclusive food and drink, or festive experiences that bring families together, we’re focused on helping customers make Christmas happen. Because this Christmas, Every Little Helps.”
Felipe Serradourada Guimarães, Chief Creative Officer at BBH London and Dublin, added: “Tesco is such an icon and this story could only have been told by them. We’re so proud to work on a brand that is able to capture the spirit of Christmas for people across the country.”
The film was directed by Steve Rogers via Biscuit Filmworks UK x Revolver and created by Pete Ioulianou and Ollie Agius at BBH London, with the accompanying track ‘Everything little thing she does is magic’ by The Police.
The ad makes its TV debut during Who Wants to Be a Millionaire on ITV tonight (Sunday 1 November 2026) with the 60’ sec edit. This kicks off Tesco’s Christmas campaign which includes the return of the ever-popular Santas’s Grotto visiting stores nationwide, and much more.

items.title: Matcha makers: Gen Z trio behind Perfect Ted fires up US expansion after Dragons' Den triumph
items.summary: Founded by husband and wife team Levi Levenfiche and Marisa Poster, alongside Levi's younger brother Teddie, the green tea brand is celebrating its fifth birthday with plans to launch in the US next year.
items.body:
Matcha makers: Gen Z trio behind Perfect Ted fires up US expansion after Dragons' Den triumph
Coffee may have powered the industrial age, but matcha will be the fuel of the artificial intelligence era.
At least, that is the claim of the Gen-Z trio behind Perfect Ted, which is taking the world by storm with its green powders and canned drinks.
Founded by husband and wife team Levi Levenfiche and Marisa Poster, alongside Levi’s younger brother Teddie, the green tea brand is celebrating its fifth birthday with plans to launch in the US next year.
The trio met at the University of Pennsylvania – far from the brothers’ north-west London roots, but closer to Marisa’s hometown of New York.
Marisa had turned her back on coffee and energy drinks as they worsened her attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and anxiety, whereas matcha was ‘calming but energising’.
Matcha is a green powder made from Camellia sinensis tea leaves, traditionally grown in Japan, and contains caffeine and amino acid L-theanine.
It is whisked into hot water or milk to provide a slower, steadier energy boost than coffee.
Matcha success: Founded by husband and wife team Levi Levenfiche and Marisa Poster, alongside Levi’s younger brother Teddie, Perfect Ted is a hit with buyers
When she moved to London to live with Levi and his brother, Marisa struggled to find matcha powder and kits for under £80.
The trio saw a gap in the market for accessible and affordable options – while Covid triggered a health ‘reckoning’ that has seen people opt for ‘functional’ soft drinks.
Perfect Ted has become the UK’s leading matcha brand, with annual profit of £4.5million as it partners with brands to supply wholesale, and moves into the ready-to-drink market with cans of flavoured drinks.
The business – which is backed by Steven Bartlett after a successful pitch on Dragons’ Den in 2023 – is now valued at about £140million.
‘Coffee was the fuel of industrialisation, allowing workers to work longer, harder, more arduous hours,’ Marisa says from the firm’s Shoreditch office in an east London warehouse. But now, for many, success is about staying sharp and proving your job is still worth paying for in an age of AI.
‘People maybe aren’t working in as physically demanding jobs as things become automated,’ Marisa says.
‘So I think matcha has the real potential to become the fuel of the intelligence age.’
But Britain is ‘limiting the upside’ of starting a business with high Capital Gains Tax on enterprise, Teddie says, so many would-be founders go into ‘the safety of a corporate role’.
‘The economics of starting a business today in the UK are becoming less attractive,’ he adds, despite the country ‘being a great place from a talent perspective to start a business’.
Levi welcomed a tax break in the Budget – so-called ‘Founders’ Relief’ – bringing in a 10 per cent rate of Capital Gains Tax to qualifying disposals of shares, up to a lifetime limit of £10million, but he said the ‘small print means many founders won’t qualify’.
And, separately, halving the limit to £500,000 at which tax breaks kick in when firms are sold was worrying, he said, adding: ‘That hits founders who fall outside Founders’ Relief, and early team members who took a risk with them from day one.’
Teddie says: ‘If you’re trying to inspire entrepreneurship and innovation, you should disproportionately reward people to take the risk to pursue that.’
Even though the Chancellor didn’t raise Capital Gains Tax levels, he adds: ‘We are losing amazing entrepreneurs, so we’re trying to be a beacon of hope.
‘Entrepreneurs need evidence that the UK is a great place to start a business where you can have incredible outcomes.
‘Entrepreneurship is such an important part of our economy that props up hiring jobs.’
Marisa says the UK is coy about entrepreneurial culture, whereas her fellow Americans are more likely to shout their achievements from the rooftops.
Win: Perfect Ted is backed by Steven Bartlett after a successful pitch on Dragons’ Den in 2023
‘I think people are very good at playing it safe here,’ she says, ‘whereas the US culture is go for it, try to shoot the lights out, try to build something incredible. If you fail, you just go again.’
Perfect Ted is keen to cross the pond next year, following other British challenger drinks brands, including alcohol-free aperitif brand Mother Root and Trip, with its cannabidiol drinks.
That confidence has caught the eye of tea and coffee giants.
For them, Teddie says: ‘You’re watching us steal share from your brands on a daily and weekly basis, as Gen Z and millennials aren’t interested as you don’t resonate with the demographics we serve, or you don’t play in the category we dominate.’
Coca-Cola has struggled to keep up with changing tastes and failed to sell off Costa Coffee for the second time this year.
Are the trio keen to cash in with a sale to one of these big firms?
‘Execution not an exit’ is the focus, Levi says. But he says the business is attracting attention.
‘People are looking to protect market share in tea and coffee, and we, as a business, are becoming hard to ignore in the tea and coffee space and energy space.’

items.title: A-listers and AI stylists: how high-street brands are staging a fashion comeback
items.summary: Gap, M&S, Topshop and more are taking a leaf from luxury label playbooks to satisfy savvier generation of shoppers High street brands that boomed in the noughties before the squeeze of both sustainably minded consumers and the rise of ultra-cheap online labels are staging a comeback. This time, rather than focusing solely on trend-led affordable designs, the names familiar to any shopper are courting luxury fashion, A-list collaborations and enhanced services in an attempt to engage consumers. Continue reading...
items.body:
High street brands that boomed in the noughties before the squeeze of both sustainably minded consumers and the rise of ultra-cheap online labels are staging a comeback.
This time, rather than focusing solely on trend-led affordable designs, the names familiar to any shopper are courting luxury fashion, A-list collaborations and enhanced services in an attempt to engage consumers.
Think Gap’s new collection with Victoria Beckham. Or Marks & Spencer showcasing a covetable catwalk collection at London fashion week with celebrities including Joan Collins and assorted gen Z Gallaghers in attendance, then making it available to buy immediately, with half of the pieces under £50. Topshop relaunched last year and now has concessions in 30 John Lewis stores, as well as the luxury retailer Liberty.
Lisa Illis, the head of design at M&S, describes their recent catwalk show as “making the buzz of London fashion week accessible to everyone”. She says “more fashion-informed seasonal collections” have seen the number of under-35s shopping at the retailer increase 16% year on year.
The Hollywood stylist Law Roach, whose clients include Zendaya, has been appointed stylist-in-residence at Asos, where his influence will be felt not just in advertising campaigns, but also through his suggestions on different items from across the site to wear together.
“In research, we found that 68% of consumers say what they need to know is how to wear something,” says Vanessa Spence, Asos’s executive vice-president of brand.
The online retailer has added AI stylists, virtual try-on tools and a Buy the Look option, which allows consumers to buy an outfit in one go, a feature that Spence says is very popular. “We’re helping customers find pieces that they want to wear. Then they can get more from every purchase and extend the life of their product.”
Ella Baynes, insight manager at retail consultants Savvy Marketing, says the shift shows brands are adapting to the more sophisticated ways consumers are approaching fashion, particularly online. “Instead of competing directly, [these retailers] are borrowing some of luxury fashion’s cultural cues,” she says. “You’re meeting both that shopper aspiration, but also the shopper reality [with the price].”
Asos’s extensive adaptive collection for disabled customers also shows this broader way of thinking. The company worked with disabled consultancy Tilting the Lens on the range. “There is an ability to develop, even for yourself, a capsule collection,” says founder and disability advocate Sinéad Burke, who has achondroplasia, the most common form of restricted growth. “It’s not just one suit, it’s not just one skirt, you can customise the pieces. You can wear the magnetic waistcoat with the pants. We hope what we’re giving people is greater choice.”
Crucially, these items are affordable – nothing is more than £65 – which is particularly important for disabled people, 46% of whom are not in work in the UK. “Whenever we’re looking at shopper attitude, cost is absolutely king,” confirms Baynes.
For Asos in particular, which registered a sharp decline in sales post-Covid and new competition from ultra-cheap brands like Shein, an overhaul was needed. Sales were down 12% last August. A cost-cutting drive, including charging for returns, helped the site turn a corner, and they announced a 50% growth of profits this March, although the impact of a cyber-attack at the beginning of October is yet to become clear.
Andrea Cheong, fashion commentator and author of Why Don’t I Have Anything to Wear?, regularly posts Instagram videos reviewing different items from affordable brands, in order to assess how well made they are. She has noticed that brands are not signposting their environmental credentials as much as they once did – due to a combination of criticism from campaigners, cost and the rise of conservatism. “It wasn’t something that was very lucrative once the economy was in decline, and then bring politics into it, that has a huge impact,” she says.
At M&S, which first launched its eco-commitments in 2007, value and sustainability are not competing priorities. “By designing pieces with longevity in mind, from everyday wardrobe staples to more fashion-led seasonal collections, we’re helping customers build wardrobes they’ll wear and love for longer,” says Illis.
But regardless of making more enduring styles, retailers are always up against changeable consumer behaviour – and damning statistics like the estimate that a garment is on average worn seven times before it is thrown away.
Even if brands are borrowing from the luxury playbook, the reality may not always match up, argues Cheong. “However much they try to elevate what it is, it is not the same [fabric] that they use at, for example, Dior.” The use of human-made fibres in ranges like the M&S catwalk collection and Asos Adaptive is just one example of the difference between high fashion and high street.
Cheong says a lot of gen Z and millennial customers are also shopping secondhand, with resale app Vinted now the third biggest retailer in the UK. “I would say 70% or 80% of my audience are 25 to 35 and they are really jaded. They are a lot more savvy than brands seem to think.”
Sustainability aside, perhaps this new shift shows that brands are realising consumers are more cynical now – and that they need to do more to reach their radar.
