items.title: What Nike’s Jordan pullback means for Foot Locker
items.summary: With Jordan accounting for roughly 25% of Foot Locker’s revenue, the athletics retailer will have some gaps to fill next year.
items.body:
Nike’s earnings earlier this month signaled a longer turnaround timeline for the activewear giant, but one of the retailer’s biggest problem areas could deal damage to its wholesale partners’ prospects as well.
The Jordan brand is a crucial piece of the puzzle for Foot Locker’s turnaround. But the most recent quarter made clear that Jordan will require more time to get healthy.
While Jordan brought in $8.7 billion in fiscal 2024 for Nike, the iconic brand is down about 20% from that benchmark. In Nike’s latest quarter, Jordan revenue fell in the mid-teens, and CEO Elliott Hill said the company would be pulling back on retro Jordan launches to correct for an oversupply.
“We’ve discussed it with our wholesale partners,” Hill said earlier this month. “Together, we will restore balance to the marketplace to create a foundation for more profitable and sustainable growth.”
In the meantime, though, that means more pain for Foot Locker, which saw comps fall 3.6% in Q2. Parent company Dick’s Sporting Goods, which bought Foot Locker for $2.4 billion last year, already drastically lowered Foot Locker’s full-year outlook in August. The retailer now expects Foot Locker comps to be flat or fall as much as 2%, compared to previous expectations of up to 3% growth.
A pullback on Jordan retro products complicates that picture further, analysts say, pinning Foot Locker’s exposure to Jordan at roughly 25% of revenues.
“If Jordan is down 30% next year, [Dick’s] has a hole to fill at Foot Locker, which we don't think can be replaced by other brands due to the [average selling price] differential,” BNP Paribas Equity Research senior analyst Laurent Vasilescu wrote Monday.
Specifically, Vasilescu estimates Foot Locker will take a roughly $550 million sales hit starting in the spring of 2027 unless it finds replacements for the Jordan volume.
Foot Locker is the largest wholesale partner for Jordan, with the basketball brand doing an approximate $1.85 billion for the retailer, Vasilescu estimates. While Foot Locker could flex up with partners like Vans and New Balance, the lower prices of those products will require Foot Locker to sell a higher volume.
BMO Capital Markets’ analyst Kelly Crago similarly flagged concerns about Foot Locker’s upcoming financials, including a cautious view of Foot Locker’s “ability to comp positively in FY27.” Crago estimates the Jordan pullback will have a 250- to 550-basis-point impact on Foot Locker’s comps that year.
“Given expected [Foot Locker] weakness, we believe [Dick’s] may need to rethink FL's cost structure,” Crago wrote Monday.
That could include shuttering Foot Locker’s European business, which accounts for about 20% of Foot Locker’s sales but is a roughly $115 million drag on profitability. Or, Crago suggested, the company could sell WSS or close down Champs.
“Whatever [Dick’s] chooses to do, we see a smaller [Foot Locker] as a further incremental risk to [Nike],” Crago said.

items.title: Value on show | In focus: Price-marked packs
items.summary: Price-marked packs (PMPs) have long been a key indicator of value for money in convenience stores. But the cost-of-living crisis has brought them more sharply into focus. As always, detail matters. Which products should retailers offer in PMPs? What are the profit margins? Is there… This story continues at Value on show | In focus: Price-marked packs Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
As always, detail matters. Which products should retailers offer in PMPs? What are the profit margins? Is there a danger that independent stores could have too many PMPs? If so, how many is too many?
Tight budgets
John O’Neill, retail operations controller at wholesaler and symbol group operator Parfetts, strongly believes in the benefits of PMPs, particularly when customers’ budgets are stretched. He says: “At a time when consumers watch every penny, clear pricing removes hesitation and speeds up decision-making.
PMPs build trust and help maintain sales volume on everyday items where shoppers benchmark against supermarkets. Demand for value will remain strong, which makes PMPs essential for competitiveness and preserving customer loyalty across core categories.”
Parfetts offers PMPs on more than 250 lines in its own Go Local range and says it tries hard to preserve profit margins, but O’Neill adds that “over-reliance on PMPs can restrict pricing flexibility and erode overall margins, especially on slower-moving lines”.
He advises that getting the mix right between PMPs, bestsellers and standard packs is key, giving retailers the room to protect profits while still “reassuring budget-conscious shoppers on value”.
Staying flexible
O’Neill adds: “Combining targeted PMPs with strong promotional activity and personal service allows independent retailers to highlight exceptional value while retaining the flexibility needed to protect overall basket profitability.”
Almost everybody agrees on the potential benefits of PMPs. Shaun Whelan, head of convenience at Link Snacks, the maker of Peperami, says: “Price-marked packs remain a vital mechanic across wholesale and convenience, helping wholesalers support their retail customers with clear value messaging and strong rate-of-sale. Independent retailers continue to look to wholesalers for products that deliver shopper confidence while also driving cash margin and repeat purchase.”
Securing prices
Within any particular product range, it makes sense to identify the key sellers for PMPs. In Peperami’s case, Whelan advises that this means the £1.25 PMP single sticks, available in Original and Firestick flavours, alongside five-packs, the best-selling SKU within the meat snacks category.
Psychologically, PMPs can also have the effect of making customers feel that retailers are making a genuine effort to help them in a time of economic difficulty.
Marta Valles Sanchez, marketing director at Takis Europe, says: “During the current cost-of-living crisis, retailers who stock PMPs can appear to be on the shopper’s side by doing the responsible thing and securing prices, which encourages customer loyalty.”
It is always worth remembering that the role played by PMPs in stores changes over time. Lauren George, external communications director at Mars Wrigley, says: “A PMP is no longer a short-term mechanic available for a set period and then disappearing.
Shoppers expect to see them, and 80% of retailers say PMPs give shoppers confidence in the price, up five percentage points on last year. This has influenced what retailers put on their shelves.
“Asked why they bought the products they did, 29% of convenience retailers pointed to the price-mark itself, up from 16% a year ago. Only customer demand and a wholesale promotion came up more often.”
Crucial moment
George adds that Mars Wrigley expects this trend to continue. Confectionery is generally bought on impulse, usually in the few seconds standing at the fixture, and a PMP minimises hesitation. Independents benefit more than anybody, says George, with 37% specifically looking to buy price-marked confectionery against 35% across total convenience.
Mars Wrigley is among many manufacturers who supply a wide range of PMPs but also advise against having too many in-store. George says: “A PMP works because it stands out from what is around it. Put one on everything, and it stops registering with consumers. The retailer has also given away the ability to price for the occasions where the shopper is not thinking about price at all.”
Considered mix
Jake Carty, category controller at Pladis, owner of McVitie’s, agrees. He says: “Ultimately, a considered mix is key. Step one is for retailers to identify the missions in-store, then step two is to use PMPs strategically, rather than treating them as a one-size-fits-all solution.”
Carty adds that finding the right balance can mean spreading your PMP range across both best-selling and high-rotation lines, together with new, standard and premium options.
Manufacturers are often helpful when it comes to deciding where and how to market PMPs in-store. Ross Davison, head of convenience at Kepak’s food division, which produces Rustlers, says it isn’t just the basics that see a sales boost with PMPs. He says: “Well-merchandised price-marked packs will even prompt consumers to purchase products that weren’t originally on their shopping list.”
Ed Merrett, wholesaler controller at PepsiCo, adds that PMPs can also be a useful tool to give new products a boost. He says: “They’re a proven way to tempt shoppers into trying new launches. In fact, 63% of new product packs sold are PMPs, which has risen from 59% over the last year.
“But retailers shouldn’t forget that sharing bags dominate this space, accounting for 73% of PMP new product sales. This means stocking new launches from best-selling brands like Walkers and Doritos in PMP format can help to simultaneously boost shopper trust and basket spend.”
As well as on new products, retailers can make sure they use PMPs to support more general trends such as the increasing pressure for unhealthy foods to be penalised and healthy equivalents to get a boost. Stuart Graham, head of convenience and impulse at KP Snacks, draws particular attention to the firm’s range of nuts.
He says: “Exempt from HFSS restrictions and backed by strong consumer demand, KP Nuts deliver on both natural health credentials, including high protein, and great taste. Suitable for a variety of needs, KP Nuts PMPs are perfect for consumers looking for a natural protein boost post-workout, or an evening savoury treat that’s great for sharing with friends and family.”
Building trust
Manufacturers can also help with specific promotions based on PMPs that can have an immediate effect on sales, such as Yazoo’s work with several UK convenience stores (see panel). Soft drinks maker AG Barr is another supplier that has increased its PMP range to boost sales. Head of category Sharon Warburton says: “We continue to see PMPs reinforcing value to shoppers and in many cases driving retail sales through offering transparency and trust.”
He adds: “The soft drinks category is one area that is particularly delivering on this. As the number one PMP category, with 40% of all soft drinks listings in independent retail being a PMP, they provide a powerful dual benefit: not only do they address shopper demand for value, but they are often not subject to the shrinkflation challenges seen in other categories.”
Harnessing the expertise of manufacturers
Bob Mulder, managing director, Friesland Campina
Several convenience stores took part in a collaborative trial with flavoured milk brand Yazoo to boost sales. The stores included Broadway Convenience in Edinburgh, St John’s Budgens in Kenilworth, Warwickshire, and Tenby Stores in Pembrokeshire.
The trial focused on increasing PMP availability alongside improving chilled displays and using dedicated point-of-sale material. It resulted in an average increase in sales of Yazoo PMPs of 89%, with Broadway Convenience managing an impressive 235% sales uplift.
Bob Mulder, managing director at Yazoo’s owner, Friesland Campina, says the company believes that, despite the cost-of-living crisis, shoppers still enjoy buying treats that are budget-friendly. He says: “In this economic climate, PMPs play a critical role in reassuring consumers who are savvier than ever about their spending. While shoppers refuse to compromise on taste or quality, they actively seek clear pricing and strong value perceptions upfront.
“PMPs directly fulfil this need by building consumer confidence and trust at the fixture, particularly within the impulse-driven convenience channel, where spontaneous pick-me-up purchases are common.”
PMPs on the rise
Lauren George, external communications manager, Mars Wrigley
Tom Fender, director, TWC
Sales of PMPs have been increasing this year, according to figures from market analyst Worldpanel, but this needs to be seen in the context of broader rises in convenience store trading.
Using the Worldpanel figures, Mars Wrigley’s external communications manager, Lauren George, says: “Convenience stores took an extra seven million shopper trips in the four weeks to 12 July 2026 against the same period last year, and branded soft drinks, confectionery and ice-cream were among the categories that picked up the benefit.”
More than a quarter of consumers (27%) say PMPs assure them they are paying a fair price, according to research group TWC. It adds that data gathered in August this year also indicates that 24% of consumers say PMPs make it easier for them to select a product.
However, TWC director Tom Fender, adds: “Suppliers have quite a difficult balancing act. They need to build in sufficient margin for the wholesaler as well as the retailer. Retailers’ cost of doing business is also rising and PMPs could be seen by some retailers as the supplier controlling margins.”
It is also acknowledged that not all retailers want PMPs. Fender says: “In some locations, the retailer could sell a product for higher than the price-mark. Also, stores open late at night or even 24 hours should be able to command a slightly higher price.”
Overall, however, PMPs are looked on favourably by retailers, as well as customers. Fender says: “PMPs play a vital role in helping convenience retailers to improve their price perception with frequent shoppers and new shoppers. Sixteen per cent of consumers agree with the statement ‘PMPs help me trust the retailer more’.”

items.title: Poundland’s future hangs in the balance as it files for administration
items.summary: Thousands of Poundland jobs and stores are at risk as the retailer has filed notice to appoint administrators. The move was prompted after the majority owners, Gordon Brothers, refused a solvent bid from Martin Property group, which increased the probability that the business could fall… This story continues at Poundland’s future hangs in the balance as it files for administration Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The move was prompted after the majority owners, Gordon Brothers, refused a solvent bid from Martin Property group, which increased the probability that the business could fall into administration.
The notice has been filed by the retail directors and, if approved by the High Court, will give the business 10 days’ breathing space to find a rescue deal.
Usdaw national officer Bally Auluk said: “It has been an incredibly distressing week for Poundland staff who have had to watch from the sidelines as a multi-billion pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1.
“Poundland’s managing director Barry Williams has reluctantly filed a notice of intention, to give the business time to find a rescue deal and prevent Gordon Brothers from breaking up the business.
“We are urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider and to prioritise a unified buyer who will protect the livelihoods of 11,000 people.”
Sean Moran, insolvency partner at law firm Shakespeare Martineau, said: “It does seem counter intuitive that a discount store appears to be heading for administration as the country remains midst of a cost-of-living crisis.
“Poundland nevertheless faces the same challenges as other high street retailers with a combination of increases to the cost of its workforce and supply costs having ratcheted due to global conflicts whilst its customers are lured by better deals offered by competitors.
“Gordon Brothers has rolled the dice and will be hoping that the administration can achieve a more favourable outcome, perhaps through a pre-pack sale of all or part of the business, than trading on in its current guise.
“This will be tough news for the staff with many no doubt hoping for a rescue package via a pre-pack that will preserve some jobs.”

items.title: Certified reverse vending machines (RVMs) for deposit return scheme announced
items.summary: Exchange For Change, the industry-led organisation delivering the Deposit Return Scheme (DRS), has published the first list of certified Reverse Vending Machines (RVMs), supporting retailers as they prepare for the scheme’s launch on 1 October 2027. Certification confirms that a machine is compatible with the… This story continues at Certified reverse vending machines (RVMs) for deposit return scheme announced Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Certification confirms that a machine is compatible with the RVM specification required to operate within the scheme, having undergone rigorous testing and assessment to reach the certification standard.
Retailers considering purchasing or leasing an RVM are advised to check the approved list before selecting a model. The list will be updated on an ongoing basis as new RVMs are certified.
Certification of the RVMs has been undertaken by a specialist assessment provider tasked with independently conducting the full certification process, which will remain ongoing to allow for new RVM suppliers to submit their machines for assessment.
Certification assesses a range of technical and operational requirements to ensure machines can operate effectively within the DRS, including the identification and acceptance of eligible containers, fraud prevention, connectivity with scheme systems, accessibility requirements and the secure handling of transaction data.
Alongside the publication of the first certified machines, Exchange For Change has also published new RVM Artwork Guidance to support a consistent and recognisable approach across RVMs.
Russell Davies, Exchange For Change chief executive, said: “Publishing the first list of certified RVMs is an important step in helping retailers prepare for the launch of the Deposit Return Scheme in October 2027.
“Certification provides confidence that approved machines have met the requirements needed to operate within the scheme and gives retailers greater certainty as they consider their options.
“Retailers considering an RVM can now review the approved list and discuss the options available with suppliers. The list is designed to help retailers of all sizes make informed decisions ahead of the scheme launch, while the new Artwork Guidance provides retailers with approved branding that can be adopted alongside their own, helping to create a consistent and recognisable approach across the scheme.
“We will continue to provide guidance and support as preparations for scheme go-live progress, including through the grant scheme available to eligible small independent retailers to support the purchase of an RVM.”
The Federation of Independent Retailers (The Fed) has welcomed the publication of the list and said it follows close engagement between the Fed and Exchange for Change, coming after calls from its national president Hemanshu Patel to share key information with independent retailers as swiftly as possible, so they can fully engage with the scheme.
Patel said: “This is another important milestone in the roll-out of DRS, and the Fed will be monitoring this list closely so members wishing to install an RVM will be able to do so once the scheme goes live in less than a year’s time.
“The specification will also be critical for some of our members who will qualify for a £6,000 grant, with the application process launching in January 2027.
“We will continue to work closely with Exchange for Change to ensure that information is shared with our members, who will be crucial for ensuring DRS successfully boosts recycling in the years ahead.”
Travis Way, managing director at RVM specialists EcoVend, part of Reconomy, said: “The publication of the first certified reverse vending machine list gives retailers greater clarity as they prepare for the Deposit Return Scheme.
“With less than a year to go until launch, retailers should now be assessing their store footprint, considering how returns will fit into day-to-day operations and making sure staff are trained and ready to manage the process. Getting these practicalities in place early will be key to ensuring a smooth transition when the scheme goes live.
“A reliable, accessible network of return points will be key to encouraging participation, capturing more valuable materials for recycling and delivering the environmental benefits the scheme is designed to achieve.”

items.title: Poundland on brink of collapse as it files notice to appoint administrators
items.summary: Poundland is teetering on the edge of collapse after its directors filed a notice of intent to appoint administrators, in a move that puts the future of its thousands of workers in doubt. The company made the filing to the High Court on Thursday, suggesting that AlixPartners, its administrators, could be formally called in to [...]
items.body:
Poundland on brink of collapse as it files notice to appoint administrators
Poundland is teetering on the edge of collapse after its directors filed a notice of intent to appoint administrators, in a move that puts the future of its thousands of workers in doubt.
The company made the filing to the High Court on Thursday, suggesting that AlixPartners, its administrators, could be formally called in to take control of the business in the coming days. A collapse of Poundland could put nearly 12,000 jobs at risk and shutter its 640 stores in the UK and Ireland.
Poundland’s American owners Gordon Brothers had been considering a solvent takeover offer from Irish property firm Martin Property Group but have since rebuffed the bid in a dispute over a loan. Gordon Brothers wanted £30m to cover a shareholder loan despite inheriting it from Poundland’s previous owner Pepco when it bought the company for a nominal £1 last year.
This appointment of administrators has triggered a 10-day moratorium on the retailer’s creditors calling in their debts, allowing it a short window in which to save its stores and employees.
Should Poundland go under, it will throw scrutiny onto the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the sale process. Martin Property Group’s bid had been backed by Poundland’s management but the Irish company had refused to cover the £30m requested by Gordon Brothers, sources said.
Three new directors – who had been drafted in to accelerate the sale process – resigned earlier this week over Gordon Brother’s refusal to accept the bid.
Poundland’s collapse would deal a significant blow to Andy Burnham’s pledge to revive Britain’s high streets. The discount retailer is one of the country’s best-known high street brands and a fixture of town centres across the UK.
The Prime Minister will also be paying close attention to the future of Poundland’s distribution centre in Makerfield, his parliamentary constituency. Martin Property Group had promised to protect this site but its security would be far from secured if the retailer was broken apart.
Barry Williams, Poundland’s managing director, said on Thursday: “Despite enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole. The process has however attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs.
“We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment. We thank all stakeholders, and in particular our people for their support during this period.”
Burnham’s high street revival at risk
While Martin Property Group was the frontrunner to buy the entire Poundland business, a number of retailers have tabled bids for significant parts of the company’s sprawling 600-store estate.
These bidders have committed to taking on the staff at all the stores they acquire, according to Transfer of Undertakings (TUPE) rules, which aim to protect employees when a business changes hands.
Lidl, Iceland, The Range, B&M and Poundstretcher have all expressed interest in snapping up select stores if the company is broken up. These firms will be on the lookout for well-placed stores and some of Poundland’s stock. A break-up of the discount retailer could bring about the end of the Poundland brand.
The uncertain future of Poundland’s employees had already prompted stark warnings from Usdaw, the retail union, who branded Gordon Brothers an “absolute disgrace” and warned the retailer was teetering on the brink of administration.
Bally Auluk, the union’s national officer, said: “The owners’ failure to accept a solvent offer leads us to conclude they want to let the company fall into administration and make 11,000 people redundant in the run up to Christmas. I urge the Government to take robust action and save thousands of retail jobs.”
Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds wrote to Gordon Brothers this week to establish the facts of the situation, according to reports.

items.title: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback
items.summary: As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming CDs appear to be having a resurgence . John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, while another report on trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are up 16%. With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit. Continue reading...
items.body:
CDs appear to be having a resurgence. John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, while another report on trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are up 16%.
With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit.
‘I have well over 10,000 CDs’
Andrew Wales, 67, from London, owns “well over 10,000” CDs. “My wife’s very considerate,” he says over the phone. “There’s quite a few in this room where I’m speaking.” They have also spilt into the next bedroom and into the corridor.
“I don’t need Spotify,” says Wales. “The fact is, I like listening to music and I have always preferred owning it in a physical form. The [size of the] CD format allows me to own the number I own despite living in a two-bedroom flat and not a country mansion, so that’s another bonus.”
Much of the classical music Wales buys and listens to is available only on CD. “I bought my first CD in 1991 – John Scofield, Meant to Be – around the same time that I bought my first CD player. LPs were becoming increasingly shoddy, both in terms of pressing and presentation, and their limitations meant that often or not songs or tracks were included on the CD release, but not on LP. There are still cases where that happens today.”
That said, Wales also owns “about 2,000 LPs”, “a few hundred cassettes” and an increasing number of Blu-rays. “I’m not always wedded to a single format.”
‘After having a baby, our records were too bulky and inconvenient’
Unlike Wales, Gabriela Crowley, 32, from San Jose, California, started listening to CDs only over the last year. “Growing up, my parents had a tonne of them,” she says. “My dad played them in the car and everywhere. And then he got an iPod. By the time I was like 18, everything had started to shift away from physical media.”
Her return to physical records started with the vinyl trend a few years ago. “I met my husband, who also had a large record collection, and we enjoyed that hobby together for a while. But after having a baby, we found we really weren’t listening to our records much any more – they were too bulky and inconvenient. My father-in-law gave us one of his old CD players and now we use that every day.”
A CD collection helps with the “paradox of choice” that streaming brings, she says. “Instead of being paralysed by the endless options, you become more intimately familiar with what you have. I find it a much more satisfying way to engage with music. Plus, no autoplay or AI-generated playlists are being forced on me.”
‘I buy CDs directly from the bands’
“I bought my first CD in 1988 and have been collecting ever since,” says Neil Cumming, 53, from Gloucester. “I have several hundred of them. Everything from classical, folk, rock, blues …”
Cumming buys CDs mostly to support musicians. “I like a lot of small indie and folk bands, who are not making a lot of money. I buy CDs directly from them when I can, which means they get a bigger share of my money than they would if I streamed their music.
“And it means I own the CD for ever,” he says. “Streaming means you are basically renting the music, and it can disappear from the streaming sites. I enjoy the ritual of selecting a CD and putting it in the machine – it is a nicer experience than just pressing play on an app.”
Not that he’s anti-streaming. “It’s quite good for trying music before you buy CDs or finding new acts. But in the evening, with a mug of tea or a glass of whisky, I find the experience of a CD more satisfying.”
‘The antithesis of scrolling’
“I am drawn to the narrative and aesthetic arc of an album,” says Asha Varadharajan, 65, from Toronto. “It’s the antithesis of scrolling. I’ve never been a fan of music as white noise in the background, unless I’m boogying while vacuuming.”
Varadharajan has owned her CD player since 1999, “which allows me to listen to five CDs at a time in any order I choose, building my own narrative arc as I listen.
“I’m grateful to friends who introduced me to artists I may never have listened to,” she says. “The patience and persistence required in listening to a CD makes songs memorable. Streaming makes music ephemeral. I think algorithms make everything predictable, but everybody’s taste is kind of random.”
It helps that CDs are hard to damage, she says. “I’m a klutz and was terrified of scratching albums as a child because I never could place the needle accurately without my hand shaking.”
‘They give me something tactile and tangible’
Ed, 63, from London, bought his first CDs in 1986 – “Genesis, Invisible Touch, and Level 42, World Machine, if you must know” – and has “never stopped”, he says. “But my interest in the format has waxed and waned.
“When they first came out, CDs were very much positioned as: they’ll last for ever, you can drill holes in them, you can put jam on them and they still play. But I got put off CDs because they sounded too bright and shiny compared to vinyl.”
But over the past two years, Ed has bought more CDs owing to their “almost throwaway prices against the excessive costs of vinyl”. Having music on CD “gives me something tactile and tangible”, Ed says. “A good digital source is now every bit as engaging as a good record player.”

items.title: Fed welcomes business rate changes but says cost of business remains too high
items.summary: The Federation of Independent Retailers (the Fed) has welcomed a campaign win following an announcement in Wednesday’s budget that the government would increase the eligibility for Small Business Rates Relief (SBRR) but has said that the cost of business for small shops remains too high.… This story continues at Fed welcomes business rate changes but says cost of business remains too high Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The announcement also stated that SBRR would be lost for those who sell vapes though the Fed has received assurances that these will not apply to those as part of a much wider range of products.
However, the Fed plans to continue to engage closely with HMT and other government departments on how this and other changes relating to business rates will be rolled out.
The announcement was accompanied by confirmation of a further increase in the National Living Wage which the Fed commented on earlier on Wednesday and comes at a time a range of commercial costs like energy bills remain high.
Despite support for consumers and industrial companies with their energy bills, there was little extra support for small retailers struggling with higher energy costs.
The government has also maintained National Insurance Contributions for a higher rate and on earnings over £5,000 per annum, following a controversial tax change made in the budget two years ago.
Commenting, the Fed’s national president Hemanshu Patel said: “We are looking closely at changes that look likely to be made to Small Business Rates Relief that could benefit some of our members.
“However, the message from the Fed remains that the cost of business remains too high. Our shops are crucial employers and also a familiar face in the communities they serve. It is important that the government continues to engage with the Fed to ensure that small retail businesses can survive.”
The Fed also welcomed measures announced in the budget to maintain the fuel duty cut of 5p per litre until July and a temporary reduction in import duties for a bundle of approximately 100 items often sold in independent convenience stores including baked beans and chocolate.

items.title: Gherkins and guffawing: Watching my first Budget, an idiot’s blow-by-blow account
items.summary: Culture writer Adam Bloodworth tried to watch the Budget 2026 in full. From the famous 4p off gherkins to the pantomime jibes, he struggled to keep pace with the childish politicians I am an alien in the City AM office. While the other journalists concern themselves with taxation and business rates, I am writing about [...]
items.body:
Gherkins and guffawing: Watching my first Budget, an idiot’s blow-by-blow account
Culture writer Adam Bloodworth tried to watch the Budget 2026 in full. From the famous 4p off gherkins to the pantomime jibes, he struggled to keep pace with the childish politicians
I am an alien in the City AM office. While the other journalists concern themselves with taxation and business rates, I am writing about theatre and restaurants. City AM’s tagline is ‘business with personality,’ and, humblebrag alert, I suppose I’m the personality.
By and large, politics and business is left off our pages – we like to take the reader away from their desks to somewhere more fabulous. And while important conversations take place over dinner, we’re concerned with telling you what to eat, where to go, and, crucially, who to put on the invite list.
And so it was new for me this year to sit through the entirety of the Budget – not just have it on in the background, but properly take it in. Here’s this lifestyle writer’s takeaways from the Autumn Budget 2026.
Call me a fish out of water, flailing desperately for validation in City AM’s hallowed towers.
Surely there was more to it than Kemi Badenoch’s take, that “the prime minister came in promising to reverse 40 years of neoliberalism. Instead we got 4p off gherkins?” Let’s see… I’m tuning in….
Budget 2026: I started with giant ambitions
I can take all this in. I can definitely take all this in. It’s basically an hour off work: watching a man deliver a speech about how he’s going to change the country. I have sat down, like millions of others across the nation, as a form of national service, to listen intently to this twice-annual sermon, only for the viewing experience to turn sour after about four-and-a-half minutes, when I had my first intrusive thought about pizza. It is, after all, lunchtime. All my hopes are quickly dashed. My mind wandering has caused me to lose the flow, and I’ve mucked this up, already. I thought I’d have at least 12 minutes in me. I can’t believe how quickly this has happened.
This isn’t going to work
This is too much information. Like, if ten minutes of someone talking fairly quickly without pausing feels like a lot of information, this is more than six times that. I really like Louis Theroux, but when I saw him say some fascinating things at How The Light Gets In festival this summer, I found myself thinking about pizza again. Sixty minutes is a long time. This is hopeless.
New approach
“You learn which bits to focus on!” my journo friend hollers from across the desk, shifting his headphones when he notices me in trouble. I can tell he’s half-zoned-out too, as he noticed me in the first place. This sounds good, and it kind of works. I tune in and have some Budget 2026 takeaways, like how “half of our shops, restaurants and gyms will pay no business rates at all”, but at other times it is still hopeless. By the time I’ve tuned back into the discourse, the Chancellor has sped ahead and moved onto something else. I feel useless, and dumb, like a stupid dumb baby.
Maybe that’s enough?
But I did learn something. I learned about founders’ relief and first time buyer ISAs and how we’re going to get 4p off gherkins, which loyal readers will know I’m very excited about. I did learn something. A lot, actually. Now I can relay this new skill to other life situations when friends bore me to tears tell me about their lives.
The pantomime stuff is so dumb
I know I’m the gazillionth person to say this, but how are ordinary people supposed to relate to the Budget 2026, and politics in general, when everyone in the Commons is literally making noises like a cow? Not to mention all the pointing and jeering, and making sassy comments. Deputy speaker Nursat Ghani told MPs they were behaving like their children, but she wasn’t much better, clapping back at one MP’s Budget rebuttal by telling him he’d “have to write yourself a prescription just to calm down”. It was one of a handful of panto villain remarks. She told another talkative MP: “I think you’ve spoken more words than the Chancellor during this statement.” It’s funny in the sense that Ghani has good comic timing, but tragic in that this Budget is affecting people’s lives and it seems like making cow noises and cracking jokes takes precedence over the politics.
The Budget 2026 is published online anyway
Don’t sweat it: everything’s published online, on the government website, minutes after the Budget 2026 speech is delivered in the Commons. So you can sit down and read it like a slow, wise old tortoise. I’d insert something here about how that’s what happens in politics anyway – everything takes forever and no one gets anything done, etcetera etcetera – but that would require me having taken in more of the Budget than I did, so I’ll just end this here. My head hurts.

items.title: Convenience curtailed: 11% of self-checkouts in London convenience stores out of action due to technical faults
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. One in nine self-checkouts in London convenience stores are out of action at any given moment because of technical faults, according to new research released today by Scalefusion, the Unified Endpoint Management company. The research, covering 730 self-checkouts in 100 London convenience stores run by four of the UK’s largest supermarket brands, found that on […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
One in nine self-checkouts in London convenience stores are out of action at any given moment because of technical faults, according to new research released today by Scalefusion, the Unified Endpoint Management company. The research, covering 730 self-checkouts in 100 London convenience stores run by four of the UK’s largest supermarket brands, found that on average 11% of machines were unavailable to shoppers. In one instance, every self-checkout was running but none could take contactless card payments, a fault that lasted for several days in a row.
This research comes as competition between high street convenience stores intensifies. Major supermarket chains have announced plans to expand their convenience store footprints. Tesco has cited new Express sites as a key driver of its growth ambitions, and Waitrose is investing more than £1 billion in expansion, with ‘neighbourhood’ stores at the heart of its strategy. Morrisons has reinforced its commitment to a franchise model for its ‘Daily’ stores, Sainsbury’s pledged more stores and automation in its 2024 ‘Next Level’ strategy, while the Co-op opened or refurbished more than 40 stores in the first half of 2026 alone.
Scalefusion is warning that, with so many convenience stores competing for the same customers, a single faulty machine will create delays and queues that erode customer experience and drive business elsewhere. The Virgin Media O2 Business Movers Index found that 38% of UK shoppers have left a store or avoided returning because of complicated or unreliable technology, rising to 51% among Gen Z. Self-checkouts top the list of frustrations, cited by 33%.
Sriram Kakarala, chief product officer at Scalefusion, said: “Convenience stores depend on quick visits – if speed isn’t possible, they’re no longer convenient. And there’s an alternative on almost every urban street. Technology now plays a vital role in how consumers experience a brand. Every machine out of action means longer queues, frustrated staff and disappointed customers.
“As convenience estates grow, supermarket chains are managing tens of thousands of self-checkouts, so a small technical fault can quickly become an operational problem at scale. A machine that’s out of action ties up staff and sends customers to competitors. Retailers need to be able to fix faults remotely and rapidly to keep downtime to a minimum, or they risk losing both customers and revenue.”

items.title: Trading Standards welcomes ‘closure of loopholes’ as new tobacco and vape laws take effect
items.summary: The Chartered Trading Standards Institute (CTSI) has welcomed the next phase of the Tobacco and Vapes Act, which comes into force today (29 October 2026), closing long-standing loopholes that Trading Standards has been calling on the government to address. From today, it is an offence… This story continues at Trading Standards welcomes ‘closure of loopholes’ as new tobacco and vape laws take effect Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
From today, it is an offence across the UK to sell any vaping or nicotine product to anyone under the age of 18.
In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, this includes non-nicotine vapes and nicotine products such as nicotine pouches for the first time, products which until now could legally be sold to children.
The public might be surprised to learn that these products were not already age restricted.
Trading Standards said officers regularly hear from concerned parents and members of the public who assume these products are already age restricted and are shocked to be told that no offence has been committed and no action can be taken. These changes put that right.
Key changes coming into force:
From 29 October 2026: The following changes seek to protect children from becoming addicted to nicotine and give Trading Standards the tools to act:
- Age of sale: The age of sale for all vaping and nicotine products will be 18 and over. It will also be an offence for anyone aged 18 or over to buy, or attempt to buy, these products on behalf of someone under 18. In Scotland, where nicotine and non-nicotine vapes were already age restricted, the restriction will now also cover nicotine products.
- Free distribution and substantial discounts: It will be an offence to give these products away for free, to sell them at a substantial discount, or to give or sell a coupon for them at a substantial discount, where the purpose or effect is to promote them. This also applies to items that promote these products, such as a vape charger with vaping product branding.
- Fixed penalty notices: Enforcement authorities across the UK will be able to issue fixed penalty notices for a range of offences relating to tobacco products, herbal smoking products, cigarette papers, and vaping and nicotine products.
Retailers who are unsure whether a customer attempting to buy vaping or nicotine products is aged 18 or over should verify the customer’s age.
The overwhelming majority of retailers already have strong age verification procedures in place, and they are encouraged to review the government guidance, brief their staff and make sure their policies now cover all vaping and nicotine products, including nicotine pouches.
CTSI has previously urged retailers to prepare for these changes, joining forces with public health organisations earlier this year to set out what businesses need to know ahead of the new rules.
CTSI said it is continuing to support businesses through this next phase, providing support, guidance and training on the new rules so that retailers understand their responsibilities and can comply with confidence.
Responsible retailers also have an important role in tackling illegal sales. Anyone who becomes aware of businesses selling tobacco, vaping or nicotine products to children, or selling illicit products, is encouraged to report their concerns to their local Trading Standards service through the Citizens Advice Consumer Helpline.
John Herriman, chief executive of the Chartered Trading Standards Institute (CTSI), said: “These changes close loopholes that Trading Standards have been raising concerns about for years. Most people would be surprised to learn that it has been legal to sell nicotine pouches and nicotine-free vapes to children, and our officers have too often had to tell worried parents that there was nothing they could do.
“From today, that changes. The new fixed penalty notices will also give Trading Standards a quicker, more proportionate way to deal with non-compliance, while robust action continues against those who deliberately flout the law.”
Kate Pike, CTSI lead officer for tobacco and vapes, said: “We’ve been asking for many years for more resources and more tools to tackle issues which people are really concerned about such as companies giving away free samples of vapes or nicotine products to children.
“We’ve now got the regulations in place, the penalties alongside, and the investment in new Trading Standards Officers through the Tobacco and Vapes apprenticeship scheme. As the Tobacco and Vapes Act is rolled out, we look forward to additional regulations coming into force in the months and years ahead.”
Eve Peters, director of government affairs for Elfbar in the UK, welcomed the new laws but called for a quick introduction of a retail licensing system.
“The new UK-wide vape rules, including on age of sale and promotion, taking effect on 29 October, are welcome”, she said. “But a retail licensing system should be brought forward to give regulators stronger tools to enforce them.
“While fixed penalty notices can be issued, retailers in England, Wales and Scotland can commit relevant offences on at least three occasions within two years before a ban on selling vaping and nicotine products can be imposed.
“When rogue retailers can repeatedly break the rules, it undermines efforts to prevent underage sales and tackle illicit trade.
“A retailer licensing scheme would give regulators oversight of who sells these products, set clear trading conditions, and enable earlier intervention without waiting for repeated offences.
“Any delay leaves a key enforcement gap unaddressed.”

items.body:
During Breast Cancer Awareness Month, M&S is celebrating 25 years working with the UK’s leading breast cancer charity, Breast Cancer Now, by spotlighting the specialist post-surgery collection and expert BraFit™ service at the heart of its longest-standing charity partnership.
Since the partnership began in 2001, M&S colleagues and customers have helped raise more than £35 million through fundraising and the sale of products, supporting Breast Cancer Now’s vital life-saving science and helping the charity provide life-changing information and support.
At the heart of the partnership is M&S’s specialist post-surgery collection. 2026 also marks 20 years since M&S launched the first post-surgery bra on the UK high street. Today, the collection combines M&S product innovation and lingerie expertise with Breast Cancer Now’s insight from people affected by breast cancer. The partnership also includes the specialist BraFit™ service and awareness activity, such as breast cancer signs and symptoms guidance introduced across women’s, lingerie and colleague changing rooms in 2023.
Supporting every customer with expertise and care – 20 years of innovation
Developed closely with Breast Cancer Now, the collection has been shaped by expert insight and the direct experiences of people affected by breast cancer. Breast Cancer Now brought together people with lived experience and clinical nurse specialists to test, trial and share feedback, while M&S also listened to its expert Lingerie Stylists and Customer Service colleagues. Their insight informed new styles, a wider choice of colours, modernised silhouettes, fabric innovation and greater versatility.
The VAT-exempt collection includes 24 products, including accessories, across 10 different styles, spanning full-cup and non-wired bras, camis and Post Surgery Pockets. The range is available in 240 stores nationwide and is designed to help customers feel comfortable, confident and supported following surgery.
M&S’s BraFit™ service is delivered by more than 2,00 expert Lingerie Stylists, who together fit around one million customers each year. All Lingerie Stylists are trained in post-surgery fitting and understand the different needs customers may have at each stage of treatment and recovery, which enables them to offer personalised support with care, sensitivity and expertise.
A BraFit™ appointment is designed to put customers at ease. There is no requirement to remove clothing, and customers can be measured while wearing a top if they prefer. The complimentary service helps customers understand their body shape, size and the styles that will offer the right comfort and support.
Charlotte Davies, lingerie director at M&S, said: “We’re incredibly proud to celebrate 25 years with Breast Cancer Now. It’s a partnership that has enabled us to support vital research while also using our lingerie expertise to make a practical difference for customers affected by breast cancer.
“Our brilliant lingerie stylists and expert Bra Fitters are a huge part of that. Their knowledge, care and sensitivity help customers feel comfortable, confident and supported – particularly those navigating life after breast cancer surgery.
“We’re grateful to Breast Cancer Now, our colleagues and our customers for everything we’ve achieved together, and we look forward to continuing this important work.”
Lucy Crisp, head of corporate partnerships at Breast Cancer Now, said: “For 25 years, our partnership with M&S has helped make a real difference to the lives of people affected by breast cancer.
“The incredible £35 million raised by M&S colleagues and customers has helped fund our life-saving research and provide life-changing support, while our work together on post-surgery lingerie and specialist BraFit™ services demonstrates the importance of listening to people affected by breast cancer and responding to their needs with care and understanding.
“We’re proud that our expertise helps M&S to be there for women at every stage of their lives, including through and beyond a breast cancer diagnosis. With one woman being diagnosed every nine minutes with breast cancer in the UK and a man every day, this support is pivotal for us to change the future of breast cancer. Thank you, M&S.
“We’re hugely grateful to M&S, its colleagues and its customers for their continued commitment. As we look to the future, amazing partnerships like this are vital to helping us move closer to our bold vision that by 2050 everyone with breast cancer will live and live well.”
With one in seven women in the UK expected to be diagnosed with breast cancer during their lifetime, M&S and Breast Cancer Now will continue working together to support vital research, raise awareness and help ensure people affected by the disease can access trusted information and support.

The plans build on Aldi’s […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Aldi has announced plans to invest a further £17.5 million in solar panels at 230 more UK stores between 2027 and 2031.
The investment will help the supermarket generate more of its own renewable electricity, with each installation capable of providing up to 30% of a store’s annual energy requirements.
The plans build on Aldi’s existing £8.4 million programme to install solar panels at 100 additional stores during 2025 and 2026, bringing its total investment in solar power to approximately £26 million by 2031.
More than 500 Aldi stores are expected to have solar panels by the end of 2026.
Jonathan Neale, managing director of National Real Estate at Aldi UK, said: “We have plenty of space on our store roofs, so it makes sense to use it.
“We want solar power to become a normal part of how we run our stores, and this investment will help us bring it to even more locations over the coming years.
“By generating more of our own electricity, we can reduce our reliance on the grid and make our stores more sustainable.”
The announcement forms part of Aldi’s wider investment in its UK stores. Earlier this year, the supermarket announced plans to invest more than £300 million in upgrading and extending existing stores in 2026, including introducing energy-saving features such as fridge doors and natural refrigerants to help reduce carbon emissions.

items.title: Grosvenor Casinos owner warns of £9m tax hit after Healey’s gambling duty hike
items.summary: Casino operator Rank Group has warned that John Healey’s gambling tax hike will deliver a hit of around £9m a year, as the industry begins to count the cost of Wednesday’s Budget. The London-listed owner of Grosvenor Casinos and Mecca Bingo said the increase in Machine Games Duty (MGD) from 20 to 25 per cent, [...]
items.body:
Grosvenor Casinos owner warns of £9m tax hit after Healey’s gambling duty hike
Casino operator Rank Group has warned that John Healey’s gambling tax hike will deliver a hit of around £9m a year, as the industry begins to count the cost of Wednesday’s Budget.
The London-listed owner of Grosvenor Casinos and Mecca Bingo said the increase in Machine Games Duty (MGD) from 20 to 25 per cent, which takes effect in April 2027, would add approximately £9m to its annual tax bill before any measures to offset the impact.
Rank expects an additional £2m in costs during its current financial year, ending June 2027, but said it remained confident of delivering like-for-like operating profit in line with expectations.
The company said it would provide further details of the Budget’s impact and its plans to mitigate the costs alongside its half-year results on 28 January.
Gambling firms count the cost
Rank’s warning comes a day after gambling stocks rallied on relief that the Chancellor had opted for a smaller tax increase than many in the industry had feared.
Shares in Rank jumped eight per cent on Wednesday, while Ladbrokes owner Entain gained more than six per cent and William Hill owner Evoke rose nearly four per cent.
Campaigners and some Labour MPs had pushed for MGD to rise to 40 per cent, but Healey settled on 25 per cent.
Entain has already estimated that the increase will cost its UK retail business £25m annually before mitigation, although it expects to offset the impact by the end of 2028 through shop closures, cost savings and market share gains.
The Betting and Gaming Council (BGC) warned that almost 1,000 betting shops and casinos could close or face serious financial pressure as a result of the tax changes, citing modelling commissioned from EY.
“This is a deeply damaging decision and a blow to the thousands of workers, businesses and communities who depend on Britain’s regulated betting and gaming industry”, said BGC chief executive Grainne Hurst.
“The Chancellor has ignored repeated warnings about the consequences”.
The increase adds to mounting pressure on high street gambling operators, following last year’s rise in Remote Gaming Duty on online casino profits to 40 per cent.
General Betting Duty on online sports betting is also set to rise to 25 per cent next April.
While the smaller-than-feared MGD increase offered investors some relief, Rank’s latest figures underline the additional costs facing operators as the changes take effect.

items.title: Phase Eight owner TFG London contacts customers as personal data is accessed following cyber attack
items.summary: The owner of Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight has contacted its customers following a cyber security incident earlier this month and urged them to be alert to unexpected emails, calls or text messages.TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - identified an incident on Sunday
items.body:
The owner of Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight has contacted its customers following a cyber security incident earlier this month and urged them to be alert to unexpected emails, calls or text messages.
TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - identified an incident on Sunday, 11th October affecting some IT systems and specifically impacting the Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles fashion brands.
In an email sent to customers, dated 28th October, TFG London CEO Justin Hampshire said: "On identifying a cybersecurity incident affecting some of our IT systems, we acted immediately to secure our systems, brought in independent cybersecurity experts, and notified the relevant government authorities."
He added: "Unfortunately, our investigation has shown that some personal data has been accessed, and we wanted to contact you about this as soon as we could. We are contacting all of our customers as a precaution. This does not mean that your information was affected, and our investigation into exactly which information has been accessed is continuing."
The information affected could include contact and delivery details, order information, and in some cases limited payment information, such as the last four digits of a payment card. It doesn't include useable payment card details.
"Our investigation has not identified any evidence that account login information or passwords were accessed," Hampshire said. "Importantly, payment processing is carried out by a third-party provider and shopping on our website and in our stores remains secure. You do not need to take any immediate action."
"However, as a precaution, we recommend being alert to unexpected emails, calls or text messages. The information affected could potentially be used to make scam or phishing communications appear more convincing, for example by referring to information about an order you have placed. As a reminder, Phase Eight will never ask you to provide your password or full payment card details by email, text or phone."
Hampshire concluded his email by stating that his company's investigation is continuing and it will keep its FAQ page updated with any new and relevant information.
"We are very sorry for any worry this incident may cause, and we thank you for your understanding," he stated.

easyShop.com, a new online marketplace from the easy family of brands, has added buy now pay later option, Klarna, to checkout across 19 European markets.

By bringing Klarna to easyShop, we're giving customers the freedom to shop in a way that suits them, while helping our sellers capitalise on one of the biggest retail moments of the year."
"The easy family of brands has always been about making things simpler and more accessible. Adding Klarna is another way we’re delivering on that, giving shoppers more choice alongside great products and competitive prices."
Klarna Interim UK & Ireland Country Lead Alex Rohloff says: "One size doesn’t fit all when it comes to payments. Consumers deserve choice, and with Klarna on easyShop, people can now pay on their terms: in full, split into three interest free payments, or in 30 days, with no interest and a clear end date.”

items.title: E-commerce brands build TikTok audiences but send viewers elsewhere when it's selling time
items.summary: Metricool, a social media management platform, has released a report analysing how 72 e-commerce brands, including BÉIS, Bombas, Ruggable and YETI, use Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and YouTube to showcase products, engage consumers and support the path to purchase.The company analysed 3,234 posts pub
items.body:
Metricool, a social media management platform, has released a report analysing how 72 e-commerce brands, including BÉIS, Bombas, Ruggable and YETI, use Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and YouTube to showcase products, engage consumers and support the path to purchase.
The company analysed 3,234 posts published by 72 US e-commerce brands across Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and YouTube between 1st-31st August.
The sample covered seven categories: fashion and apparel, home decor and furniture, consumer tech and gadgets, beauty and personal care, pet products, outdoor and fitness gear, and food and beverage/CPG.
The findings point to a disconnect between the content brands publish and how they facilitate purchases, with overtly promotional posts often performing the weakest.
Although TikTok Shop lets consumers purchase without leaving the app, organic TikTok posts were five times more likely to solely name a retail partner rather than carry a Shop tag. The report also found that results drop sharply outside Instagram: a typical organic Instagram post generated 293 interactions, compared with 74 on TikTok, nine on Facebook and eight on YouTube.
“Social media plays an increasingly important role in how e-commerce brands showcase products and connect consumers with the path to purchase,” says Juan Pablo Tejela, CEO and Co-Founder at Metricool.
“Our findings show that brands have built TikTok audiences, but when it comes time to sell, they’re still pointing viewers to other retailers instead of the shop built into the app. And heading into the holidays, the data is clear: the hard sell is the weakest thing a brand can post.”

items.body:
Bamboo Rose reports that URBN is expanding its use of AI native TotalPLM with Create, powered by VibeIQ and featuring Decision Intelligence.
The addition gives design and merchandising teams across URBN’s portfolio - which includes Anthropologie, Free People, FP Movement, Urban Outfitters, Nuuly, and Terrain - visibility into estimated product costs at the concept stage, before samples are made or suppliers are engaged.
URBN uses TotalPLM for product development, sourcing, purchase orders, and global trade management. With Create and Decision Intelligence, design and merchandising teams can see initial cost estimates as concepts take shape, helping them assess margin potential, compare options, and make informed decisions earlier. Approved concepts move directly into development without rekeying data.
“Bringing our design and development workflows together on one platform allows everyone to act on the same information in real time,” says Dan Stockbridge, Director of Production and Sourcing Systems at URBN.
“Bamboo Rose helps us simplify our day-to-day workflow and see costs earlier, so our teams can move faster and spend more time focused on great design.”
“Creative decisions shape margins long before a purchase order is placed,” says Matt Stevens, CEO at Bamboo Rose. “Decision Intelligence unlocks the value of historical data and automatically surfaces key insights within design, product development, and sourcing workflows. This enables companies like URBN to optimise margins earlier, reduce rework, and move promising ideas into development faster and with greater confidence.”

items.body:
Marks & Spencer has unveiled the first wave of jobs available at its new automated fashion distribution centre in Lichfield, set to open next year.
Over 70 vacancies are now available on the M&S Careers website, including management, operational and specialist roles. The 437,000 sq ft logistics warehouse is expected to employ 600 people in total when fully operational.
It will add additional capacity to M&S’ existing 24/7 distribution network, enabling it to more quickly process and move orders from suppliers to distribution centres and then onto stores or direct to customers. The retailer is aiming to double online fashion, home and beauty sales, with supply chain transformation a key part of its reshaping for growth strategy.
David James, Supply Chain and Logistics Director for Fashion, Home & Beauty at M&S, says: “Our new Lichfield hub will mean we can better serve our customers, delivering M&S fashion faster than ever before. As we get closer to launch, building the right team is crucial. From Planners to Team Managers and Technicians, in our first phase of recruitment we’re looking for those who enjoy the fast pace of logistics and are keen to play a role in our exciting transformation journey. We’ll recruit for more roles in the coming months as we gear up to launch.”
M&S is also investing in a new food store in Lichfield on St John’s Grange, Baker Way. The 15,800 sq ft fresh market style foodhall is set to open next March and create 70 new local jobs.
The store is one of 18 new Food stores M&S is opening this financial year, as it looks to expand its footprint and deliver larger format stores for customers, offering the full product range.

Supply chain automation will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards, which celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world, have now closed for entries. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.

items.title: ‘There has to be a bolder shift’: retail and hospitality businesses assess relief in budget
items.summary: Chancellor cuts business rates for more small businesses and limits rise in minimum wage for younger workers Budget 2026: key points at a glance “It is like letting the tyres down and then handing you a pump,” says James Nye, assessing the relief handed to businesses in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor. The managing director of Norfolk’s Anglian Country Inns argues that the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but added more labour costs for already burdened companies. Continue reading...
items.body:
“It is like letting the tyres down and then handing you a pump,” says James Nye, assessing the relief handed to businesses in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor.
The managing director of Norfolk’s Anglian Country Inns argues that the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but added more labour costs for already burdened companies.
Nye, who employs 500 people at the height of the season at its 10 venues across Norfolk and Hertfordshire, was among those business owners watching Healey carefully on Wednesday, after two previous Labour budgets under Rachel Reeves had loaded extra costs on to businesses.
Healey aimed to help high street operators by removing the business rates burden from more small businesses and limiting the rise in the minimum wage for younger workers.
The chancellor put a lid on increases to business rates, so they will only rise in line with inflation for two years, and clamped down on VAT dodging by online sellers, among other measures intended to help high streets. However, some businesses argued Andy Burnham’s chancellor could have gone further.
Pets Corner, family-owned retailer
Dean Richmond, the owner of the Pets Corner chain, says the chancellor has not fixed the “fundamental problem” that its costs are rising faster than it can increase sales.
The family-owned business, founded by Richmond’s parents in 1968, now employs 1,200 people and has 159 stores. He does not expect to get much benefit from the increase in the threshold at which business rates begin to be paid.
“It’s a bit ‘moving the deckchairs on the Titanic’ on rates. There has to be a bolder shift if the government is going to help offline retail,” Richmond says.
He welcomed the move to ensure that online marketplaces such as Amazon collect VAT from more sellers, but was disappointed that Healey did not bring forward the end of tax breaks for online sellers, such as Shein and Temu, importing cheaper items from overseas.
“It feels like the world’s against us. When offline retailers all but disappear the world will miss us,” he says.
While he says Reeves’s budgets had been “really damaging, this is safe but isn’t going to change anything”.
“It is not a good news budget with the minimum wage going up,” he says, on top of the previous changes to employers’ national insurance contributions (NICs) and big increases in the minimum wage for employers.
Richmond says the business, based in Crawley in Sussex, had been forced to make “pretty drastic cuts” to the number of people it employed and to reduce bonus incentives, and had shifted to hiring older, more experienced people as there was less incentive to hire new starters.
Herdy, independent retailer and brand
Spencer Hannah is the co-founder and owner of Herdy, which has five shops in Cumbria and sells its cartoon sheep-branded homewares and clothing online and to other retailers in the UK and overseas.
“The chancellor’s key narrative was that he wanted to support British businesses doing business with Britain and we applaud and support that,” says Hannah, whose business employs 28 people directly.
But Hannah says the budget lacked the “seismic difference” to help UK retailers and their local suppliers. He welcomed relief on business rates for smaller shops but says that was “not counterbalancing what’s happened in the last two years”.
“Like everybody else running small and medium-sized enterprises, life has got slowly harder over the last two budgets and some poor choices have been made by the [last] leadership in government.”
He says increases in national insurance contributions, the minimum wage and other costs such as rent and energy have weighed on the business directly, but the “most frustrating thing” has been the impact of the higher costs for his domestic suppliers. He has been forced to ditch some of them, such as its mug manufacturer in Stoke, and look abroad.
Anglian Country Inns, pub and hotel operator
Nye says the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but against a very tough backdrop.
He welcomes help on business rates for smaller venues but says this is unlikely to assist Anglian directly. He was disappointed that the chancellor had yet again put up the legal minimum wage from April, which will more than offset the rates change for most.
A failure to cut VAT for hospitality businesses or cut national insurance contributions for younger workers were further disappointments.
Nye hopes that Healey’s support for household energy bills “might help consumer confidence”, but added: “We were expecting a little bit more to offset the massive tax increases hospitality has faced.”
“We are being crippled by taxes as a sector and the cumulative tax burden is horrific. We pay 83% as a percentage of our profits in tax,” Nye says.
“I don’t mind paying people more, but we’re then being taxed on it because the NICs threshold hasn’t changed, and the rate of NICs has gone up, so every time that the national minimum wage goes up, we’re paying more and more in tax.
“The cost of going out is getting more and more expensive. My biggest fear is that hospitality starts becoming a luxury rather than a convenience.”

items.title: 'Go further, faster': High Street urges Labour to tackle soaring costs after Budget rates boost
items.summary: Businesses said Labour must go 'faster and further' to tackle fundamental problems with how they are taxed or help with mounting costs.
items.body:
'Go further, faster': High Street urges Labour to tackle soaring costs after Budget rates boost
The hospitality industry welcomed the 'first positive Budget in years', which eliminated business rates for thousands of small firms, but said other rising costs are still hitting the High Street hard.
Businesses said last night that Labour must 'go further, faster' to tackle fundamental problems with how they are taxed or help with mounting costs.
Their frustration came even as tens of thousands of small businesses were given a reprieve on paying business rates at all, while bigger firms will see lower than expected increases to their tax bills.
The Chancellor raised the threshold of Small Business Rates Relief from £12,000 to £18,000 for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses.
This means that 70,000 firms that 'give character to our communities' – including cafes, pubs and beauty salons – will pay nothing from next April if their rateable value is up to £18,000, with a small tapering off in rates above that level.
And larger firms breathed a sigh of relief as John Healey announced that other retail, hospitality and leisure venues would get a real-terms freeze on their bills for the next two years.
High Street: Businesses welcomed news that more small firms would receive rates relief - but said more needs to be done
This means that a hotel that has been facing up to 25 per cent increases plus inflation in each of the two years will only see an increase at the rate of inflation alone, according to analysis from property firm Ryan.
The Government said it would pay for these breaks by hiking gambling duties and forcing online giants like Amazon and Ebay to ensure sellers on their platforms are paying VAT.
UKHospitality chief executive Allen Simpson dubbed yesterday as 'the first Budget in several years to deliver any positive news for hospitality at all'.
The last two Budgets have seen retail and hospitality hit with shock increases to business rates, wages and employer National Insurance contributions.
Although there had been 'meaningful progress', Simpson said there was still 'a hill to climb' and urged the Government 'to go further, faster, to address the unequal tax burden on the sector' in order to boost economic growth and help create jobs for the young.
Ros Morgan, chair of the Real Rates Reform Alliance, added: 'While business rates relief for smaller businesses is welcome, the Government is once again tinkering around the edges of a broken system that penalises businesses for investing in premises, creating jobs and driving economic growth.'
Former Pizza Express entrepreneur Hugh Osmond said that help on rates 'won't touch the sides' as wages, energy and food costs all pile fresh pressure on companies.
Pub bosses also questioned whether the 'cavalry' promised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has a fondness for the sector and gave it a tax break in his first week, had arrived.
Greene King chief executive Nick Mackenzie said that the Budget was 'a missed opportunity' as rising employment costs and a beer duty rise 'will more than outweigh any benefit' from a previously announced 20 per cent cut to rates.
The British Retail Consortium (BRC), which represents big names from Marks & Spencer to Tesco, said the Chancellor had broken a promise to offer 'breathing space' to shops after 120,000 retail jobs had gone in the last two years.
BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson said the business rates announcement was 'smoke and mirrors' as retailers will still see a 3.5 per cent increase to bills, which she described as 'another body blow to high streets already struggling with rising costs and empty units.'
An 'overwhelming proportion' of employment and rates come from half a million bigger outlets, rather than the small firms helped yesterday, she said.
Sir Rocco Forte, chairman of Rocco Forte Hotels, said: 'The vital hospitality sector is crying out for real reform of business rates to level the playing field between online firms and those with bricks and mortar premises, not more tinkering that we saw in the Budget.'
