items.body:
THG Fulfil and CDS Superstores, trading as The Range, wilko and Homebase, have agreed a multi-year contract extension.
The deal builds on a partnership that began in 2024, in which THG Fulfil provides fulfilment and courier management services for the home, leisure and garden retailer.
The renewal supports CDS Superstores’ digital transformation as it looks to invest in technology to strengthen the online offer for The Range, wilko and Homebase. This includes Google Cloud AI technologies to improve search and product discovery on wilko.com, and Mirakl’s platform to support the growth of The Range’s online marketplace.
CDS Superstores is tapping THG Fulfil’s warehouse automation, with 95% of units sold passing through a form of automation during the fulfilment journey. This includes a fleet of Geekplus goods-to-person robots.
Tom Killeen, COO, THG Ingenuity, says: “We believe fulfilment is the centre of customer excellence and brand reputation, and we look forward to continuing to offer CDS Superstores a best-in-class fulfilment service experience for their customers.”
Ben Exall, Group Chief Digital & Marketing Officer, CDS Superstores (The Range, wilko & Homebase) says: “Digital transformation is central to our growth plans for The Range, wilko & Homebase. We’re investing in technology to make it easier for customers to find and shop our products online, alongside our expanding store network. Extending our partnership with THG Fulfil gives us the capacity and flexibility to support that growth, with reliable delivery that customers can depend on.”

items.body:
x-hoppers, an AI powered retail communication platform from Wildix, has announced a new partnership with WHSmith following a pilot.
The retailer is rolling out the platform across 300+ UK stores, starting with 32 priority locations. The first of these, its flagship location at Heathrow Terminal 5, is now live.
WHSmith selected x-hoppers to support its store teams with wireless headsets, a web app for head office and an AI powered assistant. The pilot began in late 2025 at Manchester Piccadilly station, one of WHSmith’s busiest travel locations. More than 43,000 smart notifications have been delivered to colleagues’ headsets, from store alerts and fridge and freezer monitoring to scheduled team updates and customer QR code alerts. This brings communication, alerts and requests together in one place and reduces reliance on manual processes.
In key categories, QR code notifications let customers request help on the spot, so teams can respond at the point of need. The same codes let delivery drivers contact store teams directly, minimising delays at drop-offs, and can be adapted to store-specific workflows.
Over the course of the pilot, customers made almost 1,000 requests for help via QR codes. Compared with before x-hoppers was installed, WHSmith has seen QR codes deliver a sales uplift of up to +22% in key categories.
Karl Stakes, Director of Operations at WHSmith, says: “Our colleagues need to be able to help customers quickly, especially when stores are busy. x-hoppers keeps our teams connected, so customers get help faster and colleagues are never on their own. The pilot showed what it can do, and we’re pleased to be rolling it out."
“x-hoppers was built to make retail teams more connected and effective,” says Graham Dixon, CTO at x-hoppers. “Seeing WHSmith achieve up to +22% sales uplift in the pilot and move to a roll-out across more than 300 stores shows the real, measurable value of uniting people, systems and AI on one platform.”

items.title: McKinsey research shows retailers are losing the start of the shopping journey to AI tools
items.summary: 29% of AI shoppers say AI chat or search tools had the biggest influence on their most recent purchase - three times the share citing traditional search engines (9%), and more than retailers’ platforms and AI assistants combined (21%), according to new McKinsey & Company research drawing on a su
items.body:
29% of AI shoppers say AI chat or search tools had the biggest influence on their most recent purchase - three times the share citing traditional search engines (9%), and more than retailers’ platforms and AI assistants combined (21%), according to new McKinsey & Company research drawing on a survey of approximately 21,000 consumers in 11 markets.
The shift is moving beyond discovery to influence and transactions. In the US, the share of AI users completing a purchase through AI has surged 70% since December 2025, from 10% to 17%.
Kelsey Robinson, Senior Partner, McKinsey & Company, says: "Consumers are showing unmet appetite and preference for AI shopping. Nearly a third of AI shoppers said AI chat or search tools were the biggest influence on their recent purchase. The winners this holiday season will be those that have stood up an agentic capability and are treating this as an always-on experimentation muscle."
53% of consumers across the 11 markets now use AI for shopping. China (80%) and India (76%) lead adoption, while Japan (37%) and France (44%) have the lowest shares. Despite leading in private AI investment, the US is below the average, at 48%.
Among all US adults, not just those who use AI, the share completing a purchase through AI has doubled from 5% to 9% since December 2025. Among users, the US (17%) is ahead of the global average (14%), the UK (11%), Germany (10%) and France (8%).
As the holiday season approaches, retailers are racing to enable AI powered purchases, opening their systems to authorised AI agents in a secure way. They face a new battle for shoppers as AI chat and search tools are used nearly twice as often as retailers’ own assistants for shopping inspiration (45% vs 23% of AI users respectively). But at checkout, retailers regain ground: 15% of AI users have completed a purchase using a retailer assistant, compared to 14% through a chat or search tool.
AI is also gaining ground in categories that have traditionally lagged in online shopping. E-commerce laggards such as beauty (34%) and groceries (32%), now closely trail behind consumer electronics (38%), clothing (37%) and travel (35%) as categories where AI users have turned to AI to research or decide what to buy.
In the US, 42% of users have tapped AI for grocery decisions, while the share buying groceries through AI has jumped 11 percentage points since December 2025 - the largest increase of any category measured.
Jack Trotter, Partner at McKinsey & Company, comments: “Shoppers are handing AI the legwork. They’re using it to save time, cut down their options and surface brands they hadn’t found on their own, raising the stakes for brands to be on the AI agent’s shortlist. Retailers need to be where that agent can complete the purchase. Whether that’s through product data agents can read and checkout agents can use, including their own AI shopping assistants.”

items.title: Iceland boss: Budget must show Labour is listening to business, not just managing decline
items.summary: The upcoming Budget must reject managed decline and instead foster a productivity revolution through investment incentives, skills support, and lower employment costs to help British business drive economic growth, says Lord Richard Walker I thought that working across the property, retail and leisure sectors had given me a wide perspective on business and the environment [...]
items.body:
Iceland boss: Budget must show Labour is listening to business, not just managing decline
The upcoming Budget must reject managed decline and instead foster a productivity revolution through investment incentives, skills support, and lower employment costs to help British business drive economic growth, says Lord Richard Walker
I thought that working across the property, retail and leisure sectors had given me a wide perspective on business and the environment in which we operate. Nevertheless, I was shocked at how different things were once I had a front-row seat inside government.
It won’t surprise City AM readers that I found the contrast in how decisions get made simply staggering.
In business, you can’t spend years circulating proposals between committees while technology changes, competitors move ahead and your customers expect more for less.
Yet that’s too often how we approach industrial and economic policy in Britain.
The Chancellor faces a difficult task on Wednesday. Little fiscal headroom, expensive borrowing and an uncertain global economy aren’t exactly the ideal conditions for delivering a Budget.
But there is an opportunity to do something more important if he changes the way Britain thinks about growth.
Our economic debate remains dominated by how much government can tax and spend and, but this has obscured Britain’s extraordinary strengths. World-class universities, deep capital markets, a robust legal system, language and timezone, and innovative entrepreneurs and businesses capable of competing anywhere.
I don’t believe we lack ambition. I think we’re making it unnecessarily difficult to turn ambition into investment because policy is being dictated by short-term political thinking, without a focus on growth driven by what I call a productivity revolution.
Take corporation tax.
Britain has a lower rate for smaller companies, but once profits exceed £250,000, our system makes little distinction between a growing business trying to scale up and a multinational making billions.
Surely we can do better than that?
The right approach
I’d like to see a more graduated approach, with lower corporation tax for smaller businesses and entrepreneurs investing in growth, and a greater contribution from larger companies that aren’t reinvesting their profits.
I’ve said we should use aggressive tax breaks to reward genuinely additional investment in equipment, technology, skills and jobs, fuelling a step-change in productivity and global competitiveness.
Rather than simply taxing profits, let’s encourage businesses to put more of those profits to productive use.
We should be equally ambitious about skills and putting AI in the service of our economic interests.
Artificial intelligence is already changing how businesses operate. At Iceland we’ve launched our first AI skills programme because we can see the opportunities, and we know we cannot wait years for the education and training system to catch up.
The government should give employers much greater freedom and stronger incentives to retrain their workforce as technology changes.
But investment decisions aren’t made on tax rates alone and businesses have become obstructed by the short-term policies I mentioned earlier. Bus fare caps have their place, but to invest with confidence businesses need more – clarity on when infrastructure projects will happen, how we will make work pay, and how stable our domestic energy policy will be over the next five or ten years.
We have a 10-year industrial strategy, which is welcome, but I’d go further in that we need a credible five-year delivery plan underneath it that sets a path businesses can credibly buy into.
And we cannot ignore the cost of employing people. Labour must be the party of jobs.
Employer National Insurance is charged at 15 per cent above a threshold of just £5,000. That’s a significant consideration for any company deciding whether to recruit.
If the government wants businesses to create jobs, particularly for younger people and those trying to enter the workforce, it should make hiring easier, not more expensive.
None of this means abandoning fiscal discipline. Quite the opposite. People in work pay tax, and get off benefits.
With debt interest costing around £110bn a year, we simply cannot afford an endless cycle of spending commitments without a credible plan to grow the economy that funds them.
Let’s be optimistic here and say the past week has seen encouraging signs from government of it actually listening to business. The dial is shifting.
To prove this is true, the Chancellor has an opportunity to show that Labour understands something fundamental: businesses are the ones making the investments, creating the jobs and generating the prosperity on which everything else depends.
This is a key moment for a government, which I supported for its pro-business pledge in opposition; the time to demonstrate its serious intention to make Britain a more attractive place to invest, employ people and grow a business.
So here’s to a Budget for business and jobs.
Lord Richard Walker is executive chairman of Iceland Foods

items.summary: The department store’s future is in question, but its legacy has many points of pride Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email David Jones has lived through a lot. But lately, it feels like death by a thousand cuts for the department store, whose future beyond Christmas is in question . items.body:
David Jones has lived through a lot. It has survived two world wars, the Great Depression, modern recessions and changing tastes. But lately, it feels like death by a thousand cuts for the department store, whose future beyond Christmas is in question. Not that other department stores around the globe are immune – but for Australians, this one feels especially raw.
There have been so many points of pride in its 188-year history. On that point alone, David Jones remains the world’s oldest continuously operating department store still trading under its original name. Not London’s Selfridges, not New York’s Saks Fifth Avenue – but our own DJs (as it is affectionately known).
While originally a Sydney mainstay, from the 1950s it started buying up local department stores in other states to become a national retailer. In 2016 it even opened its first international store, in Wellington, New Zealand.
More than any other location, its Elizabeth Street store, opened in 1927, is an institution. Televisions were installed for customers to watch the moon landing in 1969 and there were annual traditions including spring flower displays and whimsical Christmas windows that drew children out well past their bedtimes. Even Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II walked its floors and a state dinner was held at the Great Restaurant in 1954. It was the chicest of shopping experiences, one that drew people “into town” from the suburbs, until branches in closer proximity opened in those suburbs.
Generations of Australians have shopped from its departments, for everything from Butterick dressmaking patterns (vale the haberdashery department), to alien Alessi juicers from wedding registry lists or new doonas for the winter months. It also held rites of passage: teenage girls were taken by their mothers to be fitted for their first bra by matronly expert fitters; teenage boys were dragged in for their first suit. Mothers and daughters would once finish their shopping with lunch or coffee at the cafeteria; weekend shopping trips with girlfriends might end up at the champagne bar in the food hall.
And no Australian can look at the black-and-white houndstooth check without thinking “David Jones”. Since the 1960s, that pattern has been synonymous with the brand, covering shopping bags, credit cards, and even Megan Gale closing its autumn/winter 2007 parade in a custom Alex Perry.
Even in its earliest days, David Jones offered garments, fabrics and accoutrements in line with British and French styles of the day. But after the second world war, its fashion credentials became impeccable thanks to a tenacious buyer setting up direct lines to Paris haute couture houses. Pierre Balmain even visited the Sydney store in 1947, bringing his latest catwalk designs. The retailer set up exclusive agreements with French houses to manufacture line-for-line recreations of original designs from the likes of Yves Saint Laurent, Dior and more, making them not only available but affordable to Australian women.
Sales assistants of this era were impeccably turned out–and abundant on the shop floor. Although a work of fiction, Madeleine St John’s novel The Women in Black (and subsequent film and TV series) is widely believed to be based on David Jones.
That focus on fashion would ultimately benefit local designers, including the likes of Carla Zampatti, Akira Isogawa, Collette Dinnigan and Zimmermann. As a newspaper fashion writer from the late-2000s, I can report that the biggest news stories were built around the so-called store wars being played out between David Jones and rival Myer to sign the most coveted Australian designers to their stables. When Toni Maticevski returned to David Jones in 2019 after headlining at Myer for 15 years, it was the sartorial equivalent of a mic drop. Certainly it marked the fork in the road where DJs pursued the luxury route and Myer the mass market.
The onslaught of online shopping (to which David Jones was a latecomer), the rise of fast (and ultra-fast) fashion, a global pandemic, rising costs and cost of living means every retailer now has to work harder and smarter. But every great city deserves a centrepiece department store; and Australian cities wouldn’t seem complete without one David Jones store at their hearts.

items.title: Poundland directors quit as retailer teeters on brink of collapse
items.summary: Three directors, appointed less than a fortnight ago, have walked out following a dramatic dispute with private equity owners Gordon Brothers.
items.body:
Poundland directors quit as retailer teeters on brink of collapse
The crisis at Poundland has deepened as experts brought in to help save the company quit - sparking fresh fears for 12,000 jobs.
Three directors, appointed less than a fortnight ago, have walked out following a dramatic dispute with private equity owners Gordon Brothers.
The shake-up came after the owners, who bought Poundland for just €1 last year, turned down a rescue offer from would-be buyer Martin Property Group.
It is feared they will instead break the company up and sell off the shops piecemeal – or even let it fall into insolvency.
Poundland bosses turned on their owners on Monday following the departures of Andrew Kirkpatrick, Stephen Welch and Dominic Young.
Gordon Brothers had previously said that Martin Property Group was its preferred bidder.
The future of Poundland is in doubt - putting 12,000 jobs at risk
But the firm is now courting other bidders as Martin Property Group does not want to commit to an upfront repayment on a £30million shareholder loan. This raised fears that the new owners could liquidate the company within a year.
A spokesman told the Daily Mail: ‘The rejection of management’s preferred offer from the Martin Property Group is disappointing as it was a fully funded, ready-to-go bid that would have kept the business intact.
‘The sale process, instigated by Poundland’s owner Gordon Brothers and their advisers, continues to be a matter for them.
‘Nevertheless, it is causing an unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable situation for Poundland.
‘Any break-up stands in stark contrast to the remarkable recovery taking shape at Poundland.
‘Even though this situation is not of our own making, will continue to work hard to get the best outcome for our colleagues and other partners.’
Retailers thought to be interested in picking up stores include Lidl and Iceland, while there have also been talks with Chris Dawson, who runs the CDS Superstores group, which owns The Range, Homebase and Wilko.
Sales talks, which kicked off at the beginning of September, are continuing this week and there could be an outcome within the next few days, a source close to the discussions said.
Many of of the bids for a number of shops include provisions that mean employees' jobs would be protected if their shops reopen under another business.
But there are still worries over jobs at any shops that are not bought as well as the future of the Poundland brand on the High Street.
Should Poundland collapse it would mark one of the biggest retail insolvencies in years.
The worrying news comes as Chancellor John Healey hopes to use his Budget to win back the faith of retail bosses left reeling by a barrage of higher taxes and other costs under his predecessor Rachel Reeves.
A spokesman for the Gordon Brothers said: ‘While Martin Property Group had been identified as the preferred bidder by Poundland’s management team, attention must now turn to other active bids.
‘As well as interest from buyers for the whole business, the sale process has also surfaced a number of formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of the business from established retail operators.
'These options will now be objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders.’
Poundland has struggled with a prolonged downturn in consumer spending despite its cheap goods at the same time as it grapples with higher costs. Fewer products in its shops cost £1 compared to its launch in 1990.
Employing staff is costlier, but it has denied claims from shopworkers' union Usdaw that it is on the brink of collapse, leaving 12,000 workers anxiously awaiting an update.
The group only narrowly avoided collapsing into administration when it was sold in 2025 to US firm Gordon Brothers for a nominal €1 amid 'challenging trading conditions'. Last year, it shut 149 stores with 2,200 job losses. It now operates around 600 shops.
The shopworkers’ union, Usdaw, accused Gordon Brothers of being ‘determined to let the company fall into administration’.
Usdaw national officer Bally Auluk said: ‘Despite our repeated attempts to speak to the company, they continue to ignore us.
‘This is an incredibly worrying time for our members, and the union will continue to fight for their jobs and provide them with the help and support they need during this uncertain time.’

items.title: Bottled water and tinned food sales surge after UK government issues emergency stockpile advice
items.summary: Retailers also report jump in purchases of wind-up radios and torches to deal with extreme weather and cyber-attacks Sales of tinned foods, bottled water, wind-up radios and torches have surged after the UK government advised households to prepare for emergencies . Retailers have reported a jump in sales of items linked to preparation for emergencies such as extreme weather or cyber-attacks. The Be Ready campaign was launched last week with the aim of persuading households to lay in supplies to last 72 hours. Continue reading...
items.body:
Sales of tinned foods, bottled water, wind-up radios and torches have surged after the UK government advised households to prepare for emergencies.
Retailers have reported a jump in sales of items linked to preparation for emergencies such as extreme weather or cyber-attacks. The Be Ready campaign was launched last week with the aim of persuading households to lay in supplies to last 72 hours.
Maplin said sales of torches had almost quadrupled and sales of power banks and radios had doubled. One brand of emergency wind-up radio sold out on Friday.
The specialist technology retailer said sales would have been higher but it was low on stock, particularly for power banks after a summer of heatwaves and the fallout from the Iran war. Home security camera sales were up 130%.
Ollie Marshall, the managing director of Maplin, said: “Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics – a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank.
“These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it’s encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously.”
The grocery chain Iceland said sales of tinned products were up 40% over the weekend and it had also seen strong sales of bottled water. A spokesperson said: “It’s clear consumers have listened to the government’s message. Our supplies of these products remain healthy.”
The online grocer Ocado said demand for some products was up and it would “continue to work with suppliers to ensure there is stock for customers to gradually add items to their shops”.
Several major supermarkets said they had seen no material change in demand in tinned goods and that the cooler, stormy weather was more likely to influence demand for soups and beans.
Jim Bligh, food policy director at the British Retail Consortium, said: “While some retailers have seen a small uptick in sales for some products, food availability remains strong and retailers remain well stocked with all essential products.”
The boom in interest for relatively unusual gadgets helped specialist outdoor and “prepper” sites.
Zaid Al-Mufti, founder of survival kit seller EvaQ8, said over the weekend it had sold out of items including a make of wind-up radio and water purification tablets. He said the company had sold about 300 radios compared with the usual 15.
Long-life dried food was also in high demand but Al-Mufti did not expect this to last.
“History has shown us people’s attention span doesn’t last long,” said Al-Mufti who keeps a “grab bag” with emergency gear in his car after time spent in earthquake-prone California where such precautions are normal. “The one time demand lasted was during Covid and we also saw demand when Russia invaded Ukraine.”
Josh Pringle, co-founder of the online store Sgt Prepper, said business had been 10 to 15 times busier than usual last weekend, particularly focused on wind-up radios and long-life food including tins that last for 25 years.
“I have never seen it like this before.” he said, saying the site’s larger wind-up radio had sold out and he was having to hunt for different brands because his supplier did not have enough stock.
While the number of people buying radios and water purification tablets remains relatively low, many more households have been adding tins of food to their weekly shop.
Retail industry insiders said supermarkets had been well prepared for a surge in food and drink sales and had good supplies of the long-life groceries recommended by the government.
While pictures of empty shelves and queues have appeared on social media, industry sources warned against reading too much into the posts.
“Inevitably some people will post pictures online of an empty shelf of water, beans or other products, however the likelihood is that just out of shot is a whole load of alternatives of a different brand available for everyone,” one insider said.

items.title: Spar Scotland to host special depot open day for non-Spar retailers
items.summary: Spar Scotland is inviting independent retailers and convenience store operators who are not currently part of the Spar brand to attend a special depot open day on 4 November. It offers an opportunity to discover more about the benefits of working with one of the… This story continues at Spar Scotland to host special depot open day for non-Spar retailers Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
It offers an opportunity to discover more about the benefits of working with one of the UK’s leading convenience retail brands.
The event will give non-Spar retailers the chance to explore Spar Scotland’s depot operations, learn more about its wholesale offering and meet members of the team to discuss how Spar Scotland could support their businesses.
Attendees will be able to gain an insight into the products, services and support available to retailers, as well as learn more about the opportunities available through joining the network.
Topics will range from exclusive USPs including Iceland products in convenience stores, Barista Bar coffee, CJ’s Food to Go offering, Spar Dash home delivery, a platform via Sociolocal delivering hyper local social media pages and more.
The open day is designed to give independent retailers a closer look at how Spar Scotland works with its retail partners, helping them understand the potential benefits of the brand, its supply chain and its wider retail support.
Brian Straiton, sales director, Spar Scotland said: “We’re looking forward to welcoming independent retailers to our depot in November and giving them the opportunity to see first-hand what Spar Scotland has to offer.
“We know that independent retailers are operating in a competitive and ever-changing market, and we want to demonstrate how partnering with Spar could help them develop their businesses, access a strong product range and benefit from the support of an established convenience retail brand.
“The open day is an opportunity to meet our team, ask questions and explore the possibilities in an informal and welcoming environment. Whether retailers are considering their next steps or simply want to find out more, we would encourage them to come along.”
- Date: 4 November
- Location: Longtown Distribution Centre, 78 Longtown Road, Dundee
- Time: 10.00am
- Who should attend: Independent retailers and convenience store operators not currently affiliated with Spar
Retailers interested in attending can register their interest by contacting Craig Lynn – craig.lynn@cjlang.co.uk

items.title: Booker aims to help retailers unwrap festive sales opportunities
items.summary: Booker is looking to help independent retailers prepare for their most important trading season of the year, with a comprehensive Christmas programme featuring exclusive products, seasonal promotions, category-leading brands and advice designed to maximise festive sales opportunities. The programme, which runs from the start of… This story continues at Booker aims to help retailers unwrap festive sales opportunities Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The programme, which runs from the start of November, supports retailers in reaching consumers across every stage of the Christmas shopping journey – from last minute buys and self-treat missions through to sharing, entertaining and last-minute top-up purchases.
The seasonal support covers a range of products across confectionery, impulse, soft drinks, alcohol and grocery, responding to changing shopper needs throughout the season with a combination of new product development (NPD), Booker Group exclusives, value-led promotions and category insight.
Among the highlights in confectionery are new seasonal products such as KitKat Orange Santa and the Cadbury Dairy Milk Biscoff Bauble, alongside promotions across wine, beer and cider to help meet increased demand for entertaining over the festive period.
Nicola Cranwell, category manager for confectionery at Booker, said: “Christmas is the biggest seasonal trading opportunity of the year, with a much longer selling period than Halloween and multiple shopper missions throughout the season.
“Demand begins building from late September as shoppers start purchasing festive treats, before shifting towards sharing and entertaining occasions as the season progresses.
“In the run-up to Christmas, gifting and stocking fillers become increasingly important as shoppers complete their last minute festive preparations.”
Colm Johnson, retail managing director at Booker, said: “Christmas is a crucial trading period for independent retailers, and convenience stores are perfectly placed to capture sales from early gifting through to entertaining and last-minute top-up shopping.
“With exclusive products, festive innovation and great-value promotions, we’re helping retailers drive footfall, grow basket spend and make the most of every Christmas shopping mission.”

The achievement reflects the flooring retailer’s continued focus on customer experience as it marks more than a decade in business. Since launching in 2015, Tapi has […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Tapi Carpets & Floors has reached a major customer review milestone, reaching 100,000 5-star reviews on Trustpilot while maintaining its ‘Excellent’ rating and an average score of 4.8 stars.
The achievement reflects the flooring retailer’s continued focus on customer experience as it marks more than a decade in business. Since launching in 2015, Tapi has grown to become one of the UK’s largest flooring specialists, with more than 220 stores nationwide, including 20 John Lewis concessions, alongside a network of over 230 mobile showrooms.
The milestone comes during a period of continued growth for Tapi, which was recently named ‘Best Big Retailer’ in The Sunday Times Best Places to Work 2026 and further strengthened its position in the market through the acquisition of the Carpetright brand in August 2024.
Alongside its 4.8-star Trustpilot rating from more than 108,000 reviews, Tapi reports that 95% of customers say they would recommend the flooring retailer to a friend. The business also maintains an average Net Promoter Score (NPS) of 76.
Jeevan Karir, CEO of Tapi Carpets & Floors, shares his gratitude to customers as they achieve this amazing milestone: “Reaching 100,000 five-star reviews on Trustpilot is something we’re incredibly proud of, but what means even more to us is what sits behind that number. Every one of these reviews has a story, someone who invited us in their home and trusted us to get it right. Reaching this milestone is proof that our teams are delivering on that trust consistently.
That’s what being the flooring people you can trust really means, and it’s something we’re incredibly proud of. Thank you to our customers for trusting us, and to our teams for earning that trust every single day. That’s a commitment we intend to keep as we look ahead to the next 100,000 customers.”
For more information, please visit Tapi.co.uk/trust

items.title: Carling’s biggest brand refresh in over 30 years unveiled
items.summary: Carling has uncovered its biggest brand refresh in the past 30 years, following significant investment to strengthen the appeal of the beer with a new generation of drinkers while continuing to celebrate its heritage. Rolling out from October 2026, the brand-new look introduces a design… This story continues at Carling’s biggest brand refresh in over 30 years unveiled Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Rolling out from October 2026, the brand-new look introduces a design to increase standout on shelf, give loyal Carling drinkers a renewed sense of pride in the brand and attract new shoppers.
The new badge has already made its debut on Carling Black Label, the brand’s first new lager launch in over a decade, which rolled into stores in March 2026 and is said to have already generated £4.5m in sales across the GB off-trade.
The design will now be extended across Carling’s wider range over the coming months, creating a consistent look across cans and multipacks.
The refreshed identity will be supported by Carling’s strong links with football as the lager brand most closely associated with the sport among UK consumers.
Carling will continue to strengthen that connection this season as the Official Beer Partner of the Emirates FA Cup, alongside further marketing investment and a new above-the-line campaign platform planned for the year ahead, giving retailers more opportunities to tap into major football occasions.
Ryan McLaughlin, brand director for Carling at Molson Coors Beverage Company, said: “Core lager has an important role to play in the off-trade.
“Familiarity matters at the beer fixture, which is why we’ve retained the elements of Carling that people know and recognise, including cues that reflect our brewing heritage, while giving the brand a bolder, more confident look.
“It’s a design that reflects what Carling has always stood for: bringing people together and being at the heart of shared occasions.
“Carling’s scale means it has a significant role to play in the lager category. Following the launch of Carling Black Label earlier this year, this refresh is another step in strengthening the wider Carling range and helping a new generation of shoppers see the brand as one for them, ensuring it remains one of the country’s most relevant and loved beer brands for years to come.
“For retailers, that means a well-known lager with greater visibility on shelf, backed by continued investment around key social occasions that drive footfall.”

items.title: Bashir family opens sixth store with Go Local Wholesale
items.summary: Experienced Middlesbrough convenience store owner Bay Bashir has expanded his local retail footprint with the opening of his sixth store, Go Local Extra on Borough Road. Together with his sons Ellis and Max, Bashir took on the new 1,500-sq-ft site at 176 Borough Road, adding… This story continues at Bashir family opens sixth store with Go Local Wholesale Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Together with his sons Ellis and Max, Bashir took on the new 1,500-sq-ft site at 176 Borough Road, adding to their existing portfolio of stores in Belle Vue, Beechwood, Saltersgill, Fleet, and Wolviston.
The store will be managed and operated day-to-day by his sons with his support.
The new store, which was previously a Best-One convenience store for 20 years, extends the Bashir family’s established partnership with employee-owned wholesaler Go Local Wholesale, formerly known as Parfetts.
Bashir opened his first Middlesbrough store in Belle Vue in 1999 and became a loyal Go Local Extra retailer eight years ago.
The Borough Road store features an expanded range of convenience services, including Lottery, PayPoint, a slush machine, and a self-serve Costa Coffee station.
To mark the opening, the first 120 customers spending £10 or more received a complimentary goody bag, while the 500th customer through the doors won a 55-inch smart TV.
Bashir, said: “Trading conditions across independent retail are tough, but working with Go Local Wholesale gives us the margin protection, footfall drivers, and operational flexibility we need to keep growing.
“Their strong stock availability, sharp promotional pricing, and transparent approach let us pass clear savings on to our customers without squeezing our margins.
“Opening this outstanding sixth site is a proud moment for our family, with my sons taking on all operational and management duties.
“Having worked so closely with the Go Local Wholesale team on my previous stores, I wouldn’t have it any other way and Go Local Extra was the only choice for Ellis and Max’s first store together. Having reliable, straightforward wholesaler backing and full symbol group support makes scaling up our business much easier.”
Bay, Ellis and Max Bashir bring a strong track record of community involvement to the new site. Across his retail store network, Bashir regularly supports local causes, including sponsoring kits and equipment for Boro Rangers football club, assisting nearby schools such as Beech Grove Primary, and fundraising for regional charities including Teesside Hospice and James Cook University Hospital. The family has raised over £10,000 for local good causes.
Guy Swindell, joint managing director at Go Local Wholesale, said: “Bay is an exceptional retailer whose commitment to his community and high operational standards represent the very best of local retailing. His focus on quality service makes him an ideal partner as we continue to grow our symbol estate across the UK.
“As Go Local Wholesale expands nationally, our priority remains providing ambitious retailers like Bay with the buying power, flexible trading terms, and practical support they need to run efficient, profitable stores.”
Go Local Wholesale operates nine depots across the UK, supplying over 2,000 symbol group retailers with free membership and free delivery.

items.title: Demand for stolen goods driving shop theft, criminologist warns
items.summary: A leading criminologist has warned that shop thieves are now stealing to order, with demand for stolen goods driving the crime. The latest episode of ‘High Street Matters’ from the British Independent Retailers Association (Bira), which works with over 6,000 independent retailers across the UK,… This story continues at Demand for stolen goods driving shop theft, criminologist warns Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The latest episode of ‘High Street Matters’ from the British Independent Retailers Association (Bira), which works with over 6,000 independent retailers across the UK, features professor Emmeline Taylor, professor of criminology at City St George’s, University of London, and Andrew Goodacre, chief executive, Bira, discussing who is behind shop theft and why so many retailers do not report it. The episode is titled ‘Stolen To Order’.
Professor Taylor, who wrote a report for the National Business Crime Centre on where stolen goods end up, said thieves with a buyer already lined up get at least half of the retail price, compared with around a third when they sell after the event.
She said: “There’s an economic incentive for the thieves to establish their network of buyers before they go and target items.”
Goodacre said: “If you can close the market off for stolen goods, you do start to decrease the attractiveness of that market for the organised criminals.”
Police-recorded shop theft fell 4% to 507,086 offences in the year to March 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), after reaching a record of around 530,000 the year before.
Industry estimates suggest the real number of incidents is between 17 million and 20 million a year.
Taylor said: “I would not yet suggest that that 4% reduction actually means an on-the-ground reduction in the level of criminality that retailers are experiencing.”
Bira’s own survey of members in June found that more than 45% of those who experienced theft did not report it to the police.
Goodacre said: “There’s still this feeling that the retailers are out on their own trying to deal with a problem that has exploded in the last few years.”
Taylor also warned of the damage done by illicit shops on the high street. She said: “Every time we allow one of those illegal businesses to thrive on the high street, it is directly putting another legitimate business out of business because they simply cannot operate on such an unlevel playing field.”
To listen to the episode, search ‘High Street Matters Bira’ on your podcast provider of choice.

items.title: Why are online retailers being fined for unlawful sales tactics? Competition lawyer explains
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Charlie Markillie, partner in the Competition & Consumer Team at Knights, discusses what the recent fines issued to Wayfair, Appliances Direct and Gold’s Gym say about the Competition and Markets Authority’s growing focus on online sales practices, and what retailers should be reviewing now The Competition and Markets Authority’s (“CMA”) recent enforcement against Wayfair, Appliances […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Charlie Markillie, partner in the Competition & Consumer Team at Knights, discusses what the recent fines issued to Wayfair, Appliances Direct and Gold’s Gym say about the Competition and Markets Authority’s growing focus on online sales practices, and what retailers should be reviewing now
The Competition and Markets Authority’s (“CMA”) recent enforcement against Wayfair, Appliances Direct and Gold’s Gym is a warning to retailers: Online sales and pricing tactics are under more scrutiny than ever.
On the 14th October 2026, Wayfair was fined £4.8 million by the Competition and Markets Authority because it had falsely claimed some of its products were part of a ’24-hour flash sale’, despite them still being available at the same or lower price after the deal had ended. At the same time, Appliances Direct was fined £1.2 million for a similar issue relating to flash sale banners that falsely stated deals were limited, only for the same discount codes to keep reappearing over many days.
It’s a clear message from the regulator that it is paying close attention to practices designed to influence purchasing decisions.
Urgency claims are allowed, but not if they mislead
Countdown timers, flash sale messaging and popups are commonly used by retailers to encourage customers to act quickly on any purchases they’re considering. They are lawful provided they are accurate and don’t put unfair pressure on customers. When they cross the line into misleading consumers, the CMA can now act directly, and the penalties are significant.
Under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, the CMA can decide for itself that consumer law has been broken. It can then impose fines of up to 10% of a business’s global turnover without going to court. These cases are among the first to show those powers in use.
Automatic Opt-ins
As well as urgency claims, the CMA also investigated the use of pre-ticked paid extras by Appliances Direct, including ‘remove & recycle your old appliance’, and ‘installation on delivery’ services at checkout.
In its findings, the CMA said that customers must actively choose to pay for optional extras and can’t be signed up by default. On top of its fine, Appliances Direct must refund around £432,000 to affected customers. Their investigation wasn’t just limited to well-known brand names and businesses. Gold’s Gym, a franchise operating 4 UK fitness centres in London, advertised membership prices without including its joining fee, and didn’t make the fee sufficiently clear later in the purchasing journey either. It resulted in a £45,000 fine and the business was also already to pay refunds totalling £9,220 for 726 of its customers.
All three brands admitted the breaches and settled the cases early, earning them a 40% reduction on the fines imposed. Even so, the full cost goes well beyond the headline figures once refunds, legal costs and reputational damage are added.
The whole customer journey is in scope
The cases reflect the regulator’s growing willingness to use its enforcement powers against businesses that breach consumer law. The CMA is increasingly looking at the entire customer journey, from advertising and promotional activity through to checkout and final purchase.
One of the biggest challenges for online retailers is identifying where effective sales techniques end and misleading practices begin. Many of the practices under scrutiny are built into modern e-commerce platforms and marketing tools and are widely used across the sector, which may blur the lines further.
Retailers should ask not only “does this convert?” but also “could we defend this to the CMA?” Beyond the legal risks, people are becoming more savvy online and increasingly aware of misleading sales tactics and scams and can be quick to question businesses that lean too heavily on sales-driven messaging, whether intentional or not. Overstating the level of discount or imposing a false sense of urgency on consumers by using popups and timers can diminish credibility as a trusted business.
How retailers should respond
What retailers should do now
- Review recent promotions, especially those run outside major events such as Black Friday. Everyday “limited time” messaging is where the risk usually sits.
- Check what happened when promotions ended. Did prices actually change? Were banners and timers taken down?
- Switch off auto-repeat. Make sure urgency messaging and discount codes aren’t set to recycle automatically.
- Remove pre-ticked boxes for paid extras at checkout.
- Show the full price upfront, including any mandatory fees.
- Keep records that support your pricing and promotional claims, in case the CMA asks.
- Bring teams together. Marketing, e-commerce and compliance teams should all understand what the CMA treats as a concern.
Practices that have become commonplace across online retail are no longer escaping scrutiny. Retailers that review their promotions, pricing and checkout processes now will be in a far stronger position if the CMA comes knocking.

items.title: Nearly a third of children want to stay in education after getting a laptop, parents say
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Almost a third of parents (29%) found their child is more interested in going to college since getting a laptop, according to data from the Digital Poverty Alliance (DPA) and Currys. Two-thirds (65%) of parents also indicated their child was more motivated to do schoolwork, while 68% reported a rise in overall confidence after getting […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Almost a third of parents (29%) found their child is more interested in going to college since getting a laptop, according to data from the Digital Poverty Alliance (DPA) and Currys.
Two-thirds (65%) of parents also indicated their child was more motivated to do schoolwork, while 68% reported a rise in overall confidence after getting a laptop.
The findings come as nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training (NEETs), according to Alan Milburn’s review, with youth unemployment sitting at over 15%.
The Aspiration and Digital Inclusion report, published by the DPA and funded by Currys, surveyed teachers and participants in Tech4Families, a programme to help families experiencing digital exclusion. Its findings come as Alan Milburn prepares the final recommendations of his review into young people and work, having warned previously that fragmentation across education, welfare and employment makes it harder to identify young people at risk of becoming NEET.
The laptops provided to families enabled children to engage in schoolwork and homework, and in addition 69 per cent of parents said their children learnt new skills beyond education, such as how to apply for apprenticeships and work experience.
The share of children who could set up an email account doubled from 28% to 57%, while the share who could attach documents to an email rose from 29% to 59%, both of which are vital skills when applying for education courses, apprenticeships and jobs online.
Access to a laptop also had a significant impact for the wider household, with two-thirds of parents finding other family members making use of the device for work and job hunting. Over two-thirds (69%) said having a laptop changed how other family members see their own futures too, with parents updating CVs, applying for jobs and enrolling on courses. In almost one in five households where the laptop was shared, another family member used it to look for work.
“There are millions of children across the UK at a severe disadvantage, not just in education but in future job prospects, all because they do not have access to a laptop. Many of us take having a device for granted, but the reality is we’d feel lost without one. That’s what these children and families are facing each day, holding them back in school and their ability to apply for further education and work, which in turn impacts the job market and wider economy. Every child in the UK should have access to a keyboarded device, and that will require the government to launch a national digital schools census to understand the extent of the issue and reach the families most in need,” Elizabeth Anderson, CEO, Digital Poverty Alliance
“Today’s findings should be a wake-up call to us all. Too many young people across the UK are being held back by digital poverty, missing out on opportunities that many of us take for granted. At Currys, we want everyone to have equal access to the benefits of technology, especially when it is the gateway to education, employment, essential services and social connection. As this report reveals, access to tech doesn’t just help people get online – it can build confidence, raise aspirations and unlock opportunities. If we don’t act now, we risk leaving a generation behind,” said Moira Thomas, group sustainability & ESG director, Currys.

items.body:
Family-owned British flour brand Wessex Mill has secured a nine-strong listing at Ocado, bringing its award-winning range to the online supermarket.
Available in 1.5kg packs, the range includes Six Seed Bread Flour, Cobber Bread Flour, Strong White Bread Flour, Mixed Grain Bread Flour, French Bread Flour and Wholemeal Bread Flour, alongside Pasta & Pizza Flour, Plain White Flour and Self Raising Flour. The listing offers shoppers a broad choice of specialist and everyday flours, catering to a variety of home baking needs.
Owned by Michael and Clare Marriage, founders of Doves Farm Foods, Wessex Mill has a milling heritage spanning more than 125 years. Today, its flours are milled in the North Wessex Downs near Hungerford, where the business works closely with local farmers to source quality wheat from within 50 miles of the mill for its core range.
Combining generations of milling expertise with commitment to local sourcing, Wessex Mill slowly mills its wheat to produce high quality flour, with details of where the grain was grown printed on pack, giving shoppers greater visibility of the farms behind their flour.
Clare Marriage, co-owner of Wessex Mill, said: “We’re delighted to be bringing Wessex Mill to Ocado, making our flours more accessible to home bakers across the country. We’ve always believed that great baking starts with great flour, and knowing where your ingredients come from is an important part of that. From everyday favourites to specialist flours for artisan breads, pizza and pasta, we hope the range will inspire more people to get baking and experiment with different flours at home.”
The Wessex Mill range is available now at Ocado and from www.wessexmill.co.uk.

Asda is turning up the indulgence this festive season with the launch of Rogue Irish Cream, a new liqueur made with fresh Irish dairy cream, triple-distilled Irish whiskey and rich vanilla and chocolate flavours.
While Irish cream is a familiar favourite, Rogue takes a different approach, using cream sourced less than two miles from its production site and bottled within 48 hours. For shoppers looking beyond the familiar names in the category, Rogue offers a new option at £10 for 1L, exclusively at Asda.
At the heart of Rogue is fresh cream from a family-run dairy in Inniskeen, Co. Monaghan, Ireland, home to around 100 Friesian cows. Delivered fresh each morning, the cream can go from cow to bottle in just 48 hours, bringing a distinctive freshness to the finished liqueur.
The cream is then blended with triple-distilled local Irish whiskey and grain neutral spirits, before being infused with vanilla, chocolate and a subtle hint of hazelnut to create a smooth, indulgent Irish cream.
And Rogue is just the beginning. Joining the original Irish Cream are two further Rogue flavours, a smooth Rogue Blonde and a Rogue Espresso Martini, giving shoppers even more ways to enjoy the range over the festive season.

items.title: Why won't MPs tax the rich? We asked them – and their answers gave us hope | Faiza Shaheen

items.body:
In John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism. Or will we? Capital gains tax equalised with income tax? Ruled out. A genuine wealth tax on those sitting on over £10m? Off the table. Even the briefed increase in the banking surcharge only takes us back to where it was until the Conservatives cut it in 2023. We can cross our fingers for trailed policies on supporting high streets, financial devolution and longer-term investment, but there is still more than a whiff of trickle-down economics in the air.
Poll after poll shows that the British public overwhelmingly supports wealth taxes on the super-rich – including three in five Reform-leaning voters. We know that wealth inequality – with the richest 50 families in the UK possessing more wealth than half of the UK population – is weakening our economy, eroding our social fabric and undermining our democracy. Just last year, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, explicitly acknowledged that we have “overtaxed labour and undertaxed wealth”. So what on earth is going on?
To solve this paradox, our team at Tax Justice UK joined forces with researchers at the University of Strathclyde to go straight to the source. We interviewed 30 politicians across Westminster, Holyrood and the Senedd between February and July 2026, while Keir Starmer was prime minister. We made sure, in particular, that we spoke to every faction of the Labour party in Westminster – as the party in government and the party we would expect to be predisposed to higher taxes on the super-rich, its opinions inevitably garner more interest. The findings offer a rare glimpse into the hidden machinery of British politics. They suggest that the barrier to taxing extreme wealth is a deeply entrenched pattern of political fear, economic uncertainty, institutional capture and parliamentary self-preservation. And while these interviews took place under the former leadership, our conversations with MPs since suggest that, unless Burnham commits to higher taxes on wealth, the same barriers do hold.
The problem doesn’t start in parliament. Far from the green benches, a hostile climate is carefully cultivated to make taxing wealth seem undesirable. A billionaire-owned media apparatus relentlessly pushes scare stories, successfully tricking ordinary homeowners into thinking a “wealth tax” targets their modest family homes rather than offshore holdings and multimillion-pound assets. Outlets constantly tell us that billionaires are leaving the UK because of new taxes – even those who actually left a decade ago – and quote “millionaire flight” figures from a seriously flawed report. It doesn’t matter if they are not true – these narratives successfully penetrate the hearts and minds of parliamentarians.
Whether MPs are dismissing the prospect because they assume that the public would never go for it, not wanting to face the press backlash, or wanting stronger empirical proof covering every micro-detail of policy design and its potential impacts, this media backdrop directly undermines politicians’ confidence in fighting for higher taxes on wealth. Demands for evidence are reasonable, of course – yet we rarely see this scrutiny applied to spending on defence or AI.
Then there is the direct influence of elite money. There is a perception that when you are rich enough, you don’t need to shout from the public gallery: you have elite access. As one Labour politician told us: “If the City doesn’t like it then sometimes it can change views here in a way that’s not helpful.”
Inside parliament, this structural pressure transforms into personal paralysis. Even backbenchers who privately champion wealth taxes often won’t stick their necks out ahead of party leaders. One Labour MP confessed to keeping quiet for fear of losing local funding, admitting: “I’m trying not to be an out-and-out rebel, because I want another Pride in Place award for a really deprived part of my constituency.”
When constituency improvements are held hostage to party-line conformity, acting on principle becomes complicated. Yet this dynamic also reveals an opportunity: our interviews revealed that if the party leadership took a decisive stand on taxing wealth, most Labour MPs would fall in line behind it. Furthermore, given that Burnham has been far warmer towards higher taxes on wealth than Starmer – who notoriously referred to wealth tax campaigners as “snake oil merchants” – there is potentially more space and opportunity for MPs to speak up.
For the PM himself, this may or may not be an issue he is willing to be brave on. The danger, of course, is that the view looks very different from the inside. The retreat we are seeing suggests that Burnham and his team are already succumbing to the very same Westminster pressures our research laid bare.
One might assume that underlying some of this political resistance is an ideological dogma that taxing extreme fortunes somehow “punishes success”. But while we encountered this view among interviewees on the political right, we found little evidence of it elsewhere. Which perhaps is some cause for celebration: if many of the barriers are not ideological, there are practical things we can do.
First, we would do well to remember that winning the argument on wealth taxation isn’t just a policy battle – it’s a narrative one. As several interviewed politicians noted, the movement for economic justice must stop focusing too heavily on “who pays”, and start relentlessly highlighting “what the money buys”. People are far less interested in taxing billionaires than they are in fixing their local NHS hospitals, repairing crumbling schools and investing in green infrastructure. Taxing wealth must be framed positively as a seed investment in collective prosperity. Positive, gain-focused messaging strips away the weaponised narrative that tax is inherently bad.
Ultimately, our research reminds us that civil society cannot sit back and wait for a progressive frontbench to deliver change from above. The structural incentives inside parliament are designed to manufacture caution, not courage.
Until we make it more dangerous for politicians to ignore the public than to challenge the super-rich, we will continue to get budgets that fail to correct a fundamental unfairness at the heart of our tax system. The polls show the country is already with us. Now we must translate that quiet consent into unshakeable public pressure to push on the door left ajar by Burnham’s previously stated positions. Just like wealth, true reform has never trickled down from the top – it is built from the ground up.
- Faiza Shaheen is executive director of Tax Justice UK

items.title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
items.summary: Figures obtained by BBC Newsnight show large spikes in sales of torches, radios and power banks.
items.body:
Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
- Published
Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.
The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.
The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.
Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.
The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.
"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.
"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."
On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.
Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.
In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."
An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."
Newsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.
Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing â order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."
Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."

items.title: ETAM teams with commercetools to modernise digital retail foundation supporting brands including Maison 123
items.summary: commercetools has announced a partnership with French fashion retailer ETAM Group that aims to modernise its digital commerce and accelerate innovation across brands like ETAM, Maison 123 and Undiz.The tie up follows an eight-week MVP developed by ETAM's Digital Factory in early 2026 to demonstrate
items.body:
commercetools has announced a partnership with French fashion retailer ETAM Group that aims to modernise its digital commerce and accelerate innovation across brands like ETAM, Maison 123 and Undiz.
The tie up follows an eight-week MVP developed by ETAM's Digital Factory in early 2026 to demonstrate the potential of a modern, flexible commerce architecture against its existing environment.
Built on commercetools Sphere, with support from Algolia and Contentstack, the MVP demonstrated a 70–80% increase in development velocity, according to those involved.
"From the outset, our work with commercetools has been about more than replacing technology. We're building a commerce foundation that gives our teams greater speed and our brands more freedom to innovate," says Sébastien Ribeil, Head of Digital Factory at ETAM Group.
"The progress we made together in just eight weeks demonstrated what this approach can unlock, significantly increasing development velocity and giving us a way forward in how we can continue to evolve and grow. Just as importantly, it opens the door to new omnichannel experiences, a strategic priority for ETAM Group in the years ahead."
ETAM is now replacing its legacy commerce platform with commercetools. The API native architecture will integrate with ETAM's existing IT ecosystem while enabling individual capabilities to evolve independently, with the aim of giving its brands greater autonomy while maintaining a shared commerce foundation.
“ETAM approached this transformation in exactly the way we believe modern commerce should be built: prove the value quickly, give the people closest to the business the ability to build, and create an architecture that can keep changing with them,” says Dirk Hoerig, Founder and Chief Innovation Officer at commercetools.
“What we're building together isn't simply a replacement for ETAM's existing platform. It's a foundation that gives its teams and brands the freedom to move faster today, while preparing the business for the much bigger changes AI will bring to commerce.”
The Digital Factory used AI assisted development during the MVP to accelerate delivery with its existing engineering team. ETAM says it will continue to explore how AI can improve engineering productivity and reduce manual development effort, while commercetools Sphere enables the introduction of new AI powered commerce capabilities as they emerge.
Over time, this will support ETAM as it expands into new markets, introduces new capabilities and adapts its commerce strategy as customer expectations and technology continue to evolve.

Jayesh Bhayani has left Tesco, where he spent the past ten years and served as Chief Product and Technology Officer.
In a LinkedIn post, he said: "A couple of weeks ago, I officially retired from Tesco. When I made this choice a few months back, it came down to a personal decision to relocate from the UK, rather than a desire to leave Tesco."
"While there is quite a lot to say about commercial milestones, transformation metrics, and deliveries, I would rather focus on what actually drives an organisation of this magnitude - its culture."
He added: "Tesco is fundamentally built on great individuals and team-ship across the business. It remains one of the most authentically people-centric companies I have ever encountered. It is incredibly rare to find an enterprise operating at this massive scale that still maintains such genuine support for its colleagues. The culture here runs deep."
"To everyone across the business I have had the privilege of working alongside over the last decade, ‘Thank You’. You have made these past ten years an exceptional chapter of my life and contributed immensely to my own personal growth. I wish you my very best for the future."

items.title: Scottish retailer House of Bruar connects with Yocuda for introduction of digital receipts in stores
items.summary: House of Bruar, a Scottish luxury country lifestyle department store, says it has boosted its in-store customer experience with digital receipts in partnership with Yocuda.﻿Despite initial concerns regarding its mature customer base - the largest visitor age group is 55 to 64 years old - shoppers ha
items.body:
House of Bruar, a Scottish luxury country lifestyle department store, says it has boosted its in-store customer experience with digital receipts in partnership with Yocuda.
Despite initial concerns regarding its mature customer base - the largest visitor age group is 55 to 64 years old - shoppers have actively interacted with the new digital channel.
Highlights: digital receipts achieved a 70% open rate, over four times the standard retail marketing email benchmark of 17%; click-through rates reached 6% - nearly nine times the retail industry average of 0.7% - driving store shoppers back to online catalogues, product recommendations, and brand content; shoppers can send paperless gift receipts with personalised messages directly from their own digital receipt, thereby enabling House of Bruar to encourage gift recipients to sign up to its CRM.
Before implementing Yocuda, House of Bruar had limited visibility into purchasing habits in its physical store.
"Digital receipts have been a valuable addition to the in-store customer journey, giving customers a convenient, paperless way to keep track of their purchases while also creating another touchpoint with House of Bruar," says Ali Black, Head of Retail at House of Bruar.
"While some customers may choose to continue their journey online rather than return to store, this still benefits the business by keeping customers engaged with the wider brand and making it easier for them to shop across both our physical and online channels."
“As we run a legacy PoS, integration was the part of the project we expected to be most difficult. In practice, Yocuda worked around our existing setup, built and tested the integration on our test PoS, and we went from project start to live across all tills in just a few weeks, without needing a third-party integrator and with very little demand on our internal team," says Iain Jackson, Head of IT.
"Digital receipts have helped us bridge the data gap between our in-store and online customers, giving us greater visibility of customers who previously may only have interacted with us in-store," says John Hodge, Head of E-commerce and Mail Order.
"This has allowed us to better connect their online and offline journeys, build a more recognised picture of customer behaviour and, importantly, continue engaging with them beyond their visit to House of Bruar."

items.title: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises
items.summary: British Retail Consortium says ‘dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs’ being kept from consumers Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers. items.body:
Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.
The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.
It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday.
Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.
The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month.
Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.
Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.”
She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.
The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.
The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.
Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.
Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities, an online project working in partnership with over 200 hundred families.
She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants surveyed for the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.
One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.”
The report involves responses from 76 participants, of which 73 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month.
Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued.
“Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”
